subtopic: TRIBUTE ON PASSING OF FORMER GERMAN CHANCELLOR

May I on behalf of all hon. members pay tribute at this time to a great statesman of modern Germany, former Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, whose memory was honoured today at a state funeral in Cologne cathedral attended by dignitaries of many nations and at which Canada was represented by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin).

Today the constructive role that the Federal Republic of Germany plays in world affairs is the legacy that Dr. Adenauer has left this century in a few short years.

subtopic: CONSENT OF GOVERNOR GENERAL NOT REQUIRED BEFORE THIRD READING OF AMENDING LEGISLATION

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: CONSENT OF GOVERNOR GENERAL NOT REQUIRED BEFORE THIRD READING OF AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday at the conclusion of consideration of the committee stage of Bill C-243, to amend the National Defence Act and other acts in consequence thereof, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre raised a question as to whether this bill affects the prerogatives of the crown and therefore requires the consent of His Excellency the Governor General before it is given third reading in the House of Commons.
I referred this question to the law officers of the crown, and I have been advised that such consent is not required. The term "prerogative", according to Todd, "On Parliamentary Government in England", volume I, page 383, may be defined as expressing those political powers which are inherent in the crown and that have not been conferred by act of parliament, and which accordingly continue within the competency of the Sovereign except in so far as they have been modified or restrained by positive legislation.
The parliament of Canada has for many years legislated with respect to the organization and administration of the armed forces of Canada so that, in my view the crown's prerogative in this respect has "been modified or restrained by positive legislation" and therefore no longer exists in these areas, which are the areas affected by Bill C-243.
While the letters patent constituting the office of governor general provide that the Governor General is commander in chief of

April 25. 1967
Canada, Bill C-243 does not affect his position. Any responsibilities or prerogatives respecting the organization and management of the armed forces that may at one time have been in the commander in chief have, as I have said, been removed by successive acts of the parliament of Canada legislating on these matters.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, there is no requirement to obtain the consent of His Excellency the Governor General in respect to the introduction of this bill. May I say, however, that as a matter of courtesy His Excellency was apprised of the tenor of the biU.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT ON FIRST MEETING OF ANGLO-CANADIAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: On Wednesday and Thursday of last week a Canadian delegation led by the under secretary of state for external affairs and including the Ministers of Trade and Commerce, Industry and Defence Production, Energy, Mines and Resources, Agriculture and myself, participated in the first meeting in London of the Anglo-Canadian ministerial committee on trade and economic affairs. In the absence of both the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Trade and Commerce I should like, with the leave of the house, to table the official communique issued at the conclusion of the London meeting.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPORT ON FIRST MEETING OF ANGLO-CANADIAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Has the minister leave the table these documents?

maintopic: REPORT ON FIRST MEETING OF ANGLO-CANADIAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORT ON FIRST MEETING OF ANGLO-CANADIAN MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As hon. members will recall, the establishment of this Anglo-Canadian ministerial committee was agreed upon by the two

governments last year. While there are many occasions for British and Canadian ministers to meet, at Commonwealth gatherings at the United Nations and in a variety of other international bodies, it was felt that a joint ministerial committee could usefully supplement existing channels of communication and provide a most valuable means of consultation between the two governments. In this time of rapid change in Europe and the world at large it seemed to us that a committee of this kind with Britain, our second largest trading partner, would be especially useful and timely. As hon. members are aware, we have similar joint committees with the United States and with Japan.
Our experience has been that periodic ministerial meetings of this kind provide a unique opportunity for frank and intimate exchanges of views on a wide range of international and bilateral matters of common concern, and contribute to a better understanding of respective policies and problems.
I believe my colleagues on the delegation would agree that the new Anglo-Canadian ministerial committee got off to a good start, and that the very frank and cordial character of the discussion amply fulfilled our expectations. As indicated in the communique, British and Canadian ministers reviewed major current international issues including Viet Nam and the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons at the opening session at 10 Downing street under the chairmanship of Prime Minister Wilson. On that occasion there was also an exchange of views on the present situation with regard to Britain's possible approach to the European economic community and the important implications of this issue for Britain and Europe, for the world trading community as a whole and for trade between Canada and Britain. It was agreed that consultations on this subject would continue.
At its subsequent sessions in Marlborough House the committee discussed international and bilateral trade and economic matters including prospects for the economies of both countries; international liquidity; developments in the Kennedy round of trade and tariff negotiations including discussions of a multilateral cereals agreement; trade and aid for developing countries, including food aid, the prospects for a second United Nations conference on trade and development and development assistance in the Commonwealth, notably in the Caribbean area; and a variety of bilateral trade matters.
It was agreed that the committee would hold its second meeting in Canada at a date to be determined later.
April 25, 1967

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, April 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien (for Mr. Marchand) for the second reading of Bill No. C-278, respecting the occupational training of adults.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH THE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the time for debate expired last evening I had just finished putting on record the case for private industry and, more specifically, the case for the private schools of Canada so far as this measure is concerned. The subject of the present dispute between the department of education of Ontario and the government of Canada has been raised on several occasions. I am sure the minister will deal with it fully in the course of his remarks before second reading, and I invite him to do so.
In the course of doing my homework to be ready for this debate I took the time to read, among other publications, one entitled "Skill Acceleration", a 1967 publication of the Ontario Economic Council. This publication sets out five recommendations concerning policy in relation to long-term manpower problems and I should like to place them on record believing they are of sufficient importance to justify my doing so. The first deals with the need for additional research and reads as follows:
Additional and continued research is required to identify educational and training needs In the light of the over-all environmental factors affecting human resource development. As many of these problems are of a Canadian rather than a provincial nature, at least some of this research should be co-ordinated centrally but with sufficient regional representation to reflect regional differences. Responsibility for implementation should naturally lie with those levels of government most directly involved.
So the first point is that there is need for additional research into this whole broad field.
The recommendations continue:
One of the problems, and at the same time one of the differences between Europe and Canada, is the lack of social status associated with vocational jobs.
I remember very well as a boy in high school that those who took vocational and commercial courses were not considered to be the same level as those who took academic courses. It was as though students who took vocational training lacked the ability to do
April 25, 1967

the other. This has been a problem over the years. As is pointed out, it does not exist in Europe to the same extent. To continue:
It is not realistic to expect a young man to enter an apprenticeship program with the certain knowledge that his wages will be low for a long period of training and that when he becomes a skilled or highly skilled worker his income may not be much more than that of a man who took on a well-paying specialized job with short training periods.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Job security may be less in such specialized jobs, but this is irrelevant during a period of economic boom. Moreover, a feeling of inferiority may arise in the individual who is not able to achieve an accepted academic standing.
The attitudes of some high school counsellors and teachers tend to foster the feeling "either I'm a university graduate or I'm nothing."
Unless young people are encouraged to undertake work of a vocational nature, and unless the community accords the right status to such occupations, this problem will continue. Making vocational occupations attractive is, however, only one part of the challenge. Another is to create exit points in the educational system prior to grade 12.
Anyone who now leaves school prior to grade 12 is called a "high school drop-out," and there are too few provisions for a smooth transfer into other types of training situations.
As parents all of us have noticed that when a boy or girl does not complete high school it is considered a tragedy in the family because so many avenues are closed to the student who does not finish high school.
To provide for such exit points will require research into curriculum development and postschool programs of education and training.
One of the major hurdles facing Ontario's educational system is the shortage of vocational teachers.
Of course the shortage of teachers is a chronic situation in most provinces. There always seems to be a shortage of good academic teachers, but I know from practical experience that the shortage of vocational teachers is even more acute and more serious.
Such teaching positions at this time are still relatively unattractive, both from a status and financial point of view. Basic changes in both .monetary and social rewards are needed.
To summarize this particular point, vocational training should be upgraded. There should be more status afforded to vocational training teachers and there should be exit points provided in the high school curriculum. The third point, which I think is very well made by the Ontario Economic Council, is:
Apprenticeship and short-term on-the-job training are suffering from too great a degree of segregation. It should be possible to develop a comprehensive training program with logical exit points which would allow trainees to leave the total training system at such points.
Occupational Training
In other words, there should be a comprehensive training program but not all those undertaking it should be carried to the ultimate end of the program. That is understandable. There should be exit points along the way.
An analysis of present apprenticeship practices is indicated, with particular reference to shortening the training period. There are many practical examples where companies, particularly in Europe and the United States, are developing, in less than half the time, highly skilled employees of equal or better competence than those graduating from apprenticeship programs.
We are familiar, of course, with the old principle of British apprenticeship under which young lads went into the shipyards of the Clyde, Newcastle-on-Tyne and Aberdeen-at the last place I had the opportunity to see them at one time-at the ages of 12 or 13 and spent from five to seven years as apprentices. It was a long, thorough apprenticeship-I think perhaps too long because they were paid practically nothing. But the net result was that the shipbuilders who were developed on the Clyde and the Tyne were known all over the world. The Scottish marine engineer is one of the most highly skilled men at his trade anywhere in the world.
In effect the third point which is made is that we could very well do with shorter courses. I think the last two points are very important because they deal with the part which private industry and labour should play in this whole matter that we are discussing today.
Industry and commerce must assume a greater responsibility for the development of operating skills.
Of course the bill encourages this.
The costs of "raiding" could be alleviated, at least in part, by providing tax incentives or subsidies to companies for educational programs, including such activities as vestibule training or non-production on-the-premises training.
I am not quite certain what is meant by vestibule training, but non-production on-the-premises training is self-explanatory.
Such a policy would invalidate the oft-repeated argument that employees are only trained for other companies.
I know the minister is aware of this because in his remarks on the resolution this matter was raised.
Management and supervision could also be given more direct responsibility for training. There is a variety of sound, on-the-job training programs which utilize either supervisors or experienced employees for instructional purposes.

April 25, 1967'
Occupational Training
In other words, the fourth point in these recommendations is that industry should become much more involved than it has up to the present.
The final point deals with labour. Just today during the noon hour many of us met with Canadian shoe manufacturers who are facing a real problem because of low cost imports of shoes and boots. I could not help but he impressed, and I said so during the course of the discussion with the large group present, that labour was well represented. Representatives of the labour unions in the shoe industry attended. That is a good thing. They seemed to be deeply conscientious and aware of what was happening and were anxious to help the industry with this problem. The fifth point in the recommendations is:
A major challenge In vocational development falls upon organized labour. The welfare of the union member can no longer be related to shortterm contracts. Moreover restrictions applying to job transfers in contracts do not, in the long run, make economic sense for individual employees. Organized labour could make a genuine contribution through a re-evaluation of such points as they relate to:
(a)	the need for including education in job responsibilities;
(b)	the real needs to be served by apprenticeship programs;
(c)	the opportunities for employers and union members to benefit from individual educational efforts.
The article concludes.
Such re-evaluations have already resulted in unofficial changes in practices in many locals. This practical proof could well be recognized in terms of official policy.
It has been said, Mr. Speaker, that the machines that will do the world's work 25 years from now have not yet been invented. I believe that. It has also been said that a very large proportion of our working force today will not complete their working years at the skills in which they are now employed. That is true, and that is the whole purpose of what we are here for this afternoon.
I said at the beginning of my remarks that this measure is one of the most important to come before the house for many years because it deals with the lives and the livelihood not only of our people today but of those generations to come, and for that reason it is vitally important. I may disagree with some of the provisions included in the measure when we reach them. As the minister knows, I have an amendment to submit. I hope he will look upon it favourably. I understand the principles of government of course

but I would ask him to look at my amendment carefully. I wish him well on this measure, and I also wish the government well because in wishing the government well I am wishing the people of this country well, and' that is what we are here in this house to do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH THE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his opening statement yesterday the parliamentary secretary endeavoured to make this bill controversial by insinuating that the opposition has delayed its passage by discussing, the unification bill and, I might also add, by discussing the medicare bill. We would have welcomed this bill's appearance on the order paper much earlier, and had the government given priority to it the other two bills I have mentioned could have been dealt with subsequently. I can only say that there has been poor government planning in this regard.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Because of the haste with which these adult training courses were initiated no definite regulations were established and no proper organization was set up to deal with this program. I believe that the 100 letters I have on file justify the statement on my part that no proper organization was set up before these adult training courses were established. Many people believe themselves to be discriminated against. A good deal of explaining will have to be done to justify the position which has been taken in respect of these people. The blame in this regard can only be attributed to the minister. No planning or study sessions were held with the provincial governments or with the educators and the managers of the manpower centres. Although I was informed that the selection committee in each region would be made up of the manpower centre manager, the chairman of the regional school board and the head of the local school board, this apparently has not been the case and the managers have had to carry on alone.
I have no right to speak about the qualifications of the managers. I do, however, ask myself whether the manager of a manpower centre who is placed in this position can take a decision with regard to whether or not a person can qualify for these courses. Had the program been properly organized with the school board authorities, either local or regional, I am sure that a more proper assessment could have been made of the eligibility of persons. In this way many of the criticisms which have been made and the impressions which people still have to live with could have been eliminated. These
April 25, 1967

procedures which were adopted in haste have caused an undue strain, serious emotional stress and financial loss to many people who are able to qualify.
As has been mentioned by the parliamentary secretary, this measure provides that the government will be the financial agent for the hundreds of thousands of Canadian workers whose future earnings are dependent on more training. He went on to say that this is not a form of relief. I would love to believe this. Many of these people do not even receive unemployment benefits because they cannot qualify for them. These people are the recipients of social allowances. They did not find sufficient employment during the year to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits and therefore found it necessary to apply to social agencies in order to obtain some of the money necessary to support their families.
The minute either a husband or wife qualifies for these courses the social allowances which have been paid to them are cut off. In many cases many of those who attend these courses are not available to the labour market. This can be proven in respect of many regions. Of course I speak mostly of the rural areas of the country. Those who did qualify received these payments which were agreed to by the provincial authorities. However, many who were unable to qualify for these courses have been deprived of an education which would have made it possible for them to obtain better employment.
I am all in favour of upgrading the training and education of these people. I am wondering, however, whether the practice which has been followed this past winter will solve the problems. We are moving ahead and entering into the courses when no firm regulations have been laid down. Most of the people who enter these schools are receiving social allowances rather than unemployment insurance. Therefore we are bringing to the schools people who possibly never will be available for the labour market. In this manner we are depriving those people who could get into the labour market of the opportunity to attend these courses and receive this assistance.
I understand that the agreement concerning where and how these courses will be given, as well as the amount of the allowances which may range from $35 a week to $90 a week, is made with the provincial authorities. The allowances are based on the average revenue in each district. I find it difficult to understand why the national government which is paying the shot should allow a province to determine exactly what amount of money should be
Occupational Training
paid. Is there any reason why a person who is living in an outlying district and attending these courses should be paid $35 a week while another person living in a different area is entitled to $50 or $60 a week? I believe this is very unfair to those who in order to upgrade themselves wish to attend these courses. There is discrimination at the national level which extends through the provincial level.
If we are to pay for these courses, then I believe the same rate of payment should be available to all Canadians whether they come from one part of the country or another. I cannot understand how there can be any justification for the fact that different rates are payable across the country. I believe there is discrimination because, as I said before, I do not believe the manager of a manpower training centre alone is qualified to decide who should attend these courses. I should like to quote from a brief submitted by C. H. Rush-ton, co-ordinator, Ontario manpower retraining program:
The Department of Manpower and Immigration, and the provincial department of education are having serious difficulties in co-operating due to the fact that Canada manpower centres are neither knowledgeable nor humane in respect to the educating and training of individuals. Is the minister aware of the fact that persons are being directed to training by placement officers who have no more than grade 10 education? The staffs in many local manpower centres are totally inadequate in so far as training and qualifications are concerned to determine whether or not a man has the academic qualifications to enrol in a skill training program. The minister himself would be hard pressed to determine, in a twenty or forty minute interview, whether or not an individual requiring skill training is functioning at a grade 10 level. Nevertheless, in their ignorance, local manpower placement officers are being instructed to make judgments of a nature which educationalists with years of training and experience would not dare to make without comprehensive testing and counselling.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
This is exactly what I have been referring to. I believe that those people who will occupy positions in the manpower centres across the country should be properly prepared and educated to enable them to interview and assess the value of those applying for the right to attend these courses, whether they are courses in adult education or vocational training.
I should like to quote now from a speech made by the minister in Ottawa on February 21, 1966. He said:

In spite of the prosperity experienced by Canada, there is still poverty in many localities; in several areas the standard of living is inferior

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
to the national average and too many people lead sterile and degrading lives either because of their age, their lack of education, physical handicaps, or because they are unable to find decent and remunerative employment. Our ideal of justice and equality demands that we give every citizen the means to lead an honourable life, not for some altruistic reason or other, but due to the obligation we have of using to the maximum all the energies at our disposal.

I believe no one can disagree with those words. I believe also that the minister is very-sincere in lacing up to the problems of unemployment and preparing our people, especially our youth, by means of an education which will permit them to enter into many spheres of industrial operations. However, I do not know how we are going to solve this problem in the rural areas of our country, and I am not certain the minister knows. Not many of our legislators come from the urban areas of our country and are competent to deal with the problems there. How many of those who work with the minister or with the heads of the departments are familiar with the problems which exist in the rural areas of the country? I am speaking now of all the rural areas because that is where we most often find chronic unemployment, with people having been unemployed for years and having no hope of finding a job anywhere in this country. As I said, I do not know what the solution to this problem will be, but one thing is definitely clear to me, that we should concern ourselves with helping these people to find employment and preparing them for it.
There are many pockets of unemployment across the country where people look to the future with dismay and a lack of hope of ever being able to do what others seem to be able to do. This is a very distressing situation. Above all, we must think of those who are chronically unemployed because they must not be allowed to face the future knowing they will have to depend on welfare benefits for the rest of their lives.
I am not speaking strictly of this government but of governments in general. I believe there is a lack of co-ordination not only among ministers but among their departments. It seems that the right hand of government knows not what the left hand is doing. There is a duplication of efforts.
At this point I should like to suggest a few of the areas where duplication exists. We know that at present there is a housing problem in this country. It is a problem that faces Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which is answerable to parliament through
[Mr. Keays.l
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson). At the same time the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing) is preoccupied with the problem of housing in the national parks, and the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauve) is dealing with housing under the ARDA program. It seems to me that we are leaving the main street and entering many side streets from which there is no return. We are not concentrating our efforts in one direction. If we wish to solve the housing problem the efforts of all the departments concerned should be directed toward that objective.
Again I am reminded of the time last year when the government, in co-operation with private industry, announced that a heavy water plant was going to be built in Nova Scotia. I have no objection to that but I do object to a second heavy water plant being built in the same province when other areas of Canada with the highest rate of unemployment in the country, areas which could offer the same natural resources and all the labour needed to operate a heavy water plant, have been overlooked. I think it was the government's responsibility to establish the second heavy water plant in an area of chronic unemployment. This is where the government has fallen down. The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, for example, does not seem to be aware of the problems facing the Department of Labour and the Department of Manpower and Immigration. If the efforts of all the departments had been directed toward solving this problem the second heavy water plant might have been established in the Gaspe.
Another matter that comes to my mind concerns the most natural harbour in the world which is to be found in the Gaspe and today is being wasted because we cannot find any use for it. First of all, we should try to establish industries in these areas so that those people whom we are helping to prepare themselves for employment will know that they will be able to find it when they complete their training. At present they are preparing themselves to return to school for another year without the hope of finding employment later. This is a sad situation.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I am in favour of adult education and vocational training and I agree we must prepare our people for future employment. However,
I cannot understand why only one out of four factories in this country provides any training whatsoever. It has been said that employers
April 25, 1967

feel they will be training people for their competitors. Those who operate factories and large corporations are supposedly intelligent people and they must know that they have a part to play in the whole problem of employment. They should be told that they must also train people whether or not they lose some of their trainees, because the end result of this program will be increased productivity in our country. This will improve our position in the economic field where for the last ten years we have ranked as the fourteenth nation in terms of real productivity.
There is an obligation on government and employers in this respect. They must realize that we will not remain competitive if we take a lackadaisical attitude toward productivity. Increased productivity will be attained by increased education. We must tell corporations and employers that they have a part to play, and they must know that a program of this type is also for their own good. All the blame should not be placed on the employers. On two occasions recently I have spoken to union leaders and told them that they should not concern themselves only with getting members for their unions, that they should not spend their time fighting each other but should undertake a program of education for their members and show them that increased salaries will only be brought about and justified by increased productivity. This is not a one-way street. It is quite important that both parties play their part and give to this country a better competitive position than we have today.
I do not intend to speak any longer on this subject. I endorse this legislation in part but hope that in view of the developments of the past winter the government will learn a lesson and never introduce or put new legislation into effect unless preparatory work has been carried out so that justice may be done to all those who are eligible for employment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH THE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make some remarks on this bill in the context of the new government policy in regard to education and training and then I shall make some comments about the specific provisions of the bill. The bill arises from decisions taken by the federal government after the federal-provincial conference of last fall. Apparently the main decisions were taken by the federal government on its own. They consulted the provinces but it seems to me that the major decisions were handed to the provinces by the federal government. In place of the former policy of
Occupational Training
co-operative federalism we have had what might be called unilateral federalism.
What were these main decisions concerning education and retraining that were taken at the conference last fall? First of all there was the decision of the federal government to withdraw from what they call the field of education and concern themselves only with what they call training. They made a distinction between education and training. It was an arbitrary decision, and had to be. People who have worked for years in the field of education have not been able to make this distinction, but it has been made in this instance.
Apparently education is a process which takes place in the elementary and secondary schools and colleges and universities, and is to be paid for in the future by the provincial governments. The federal government, of course, is transferring certain percentage points of taxes to the provinces to assist them in what is called education. Training is something which takes place not in the schools but is for adults, people who have been out of school for at least three years, if they are single, or for a lesser period of time if they have dependants. So we have this distinction between education and training. I think it is a rather false distinction and a very hard one to make. Hence it had to be a quite arbitrary decision.
It was an arbitrary decision and it was not in the spirit of the co-operative federalism we have heard about in Ottawa for the past several years. This is not an easy term to define. I have a whole file of speeches made by Mr. Favreau, Mr. Lamontagne and the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) who have been going around the country explaining co-operative federalism. I would think that among other things it certainly means co-operating with the provinces on joint programs. However, I shall refer to some of the definitions used and relate them to this subject. I shall first quote from a speech made by Mr. Favreau on October 20, 1964, to the Chamber of Commerce of Montreal. H<* had this to say:
For we believe that the indispensable counterpart of provincial autonomy is a permanent interdependence of the provincial and federal governments. This interdependence grows first from the participation of all these governments in a common monetary and trading system; but it is necessary also because many of the fields of jurisdiction that our constitution has distributed to Ottawa and the provinces are complementary or concurrent. One need only study any aspect of our federal foreign policy-immigration, defence, cultural relations, trade-to catch the reflection

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
of problems which preoccupy, in the first instance, the provinces; unemployment, industrialization, education and productivity.
I would point out that he used the word "education". Then he said:
And of course, the influence of provincial policies on those of Ottawa is at least as powerful. By the very complexity of our federalism, the provincial and federal states are called upon to recognize their deep and inevitable solidarity.
But, one may ask, how can you express this solidarity without threatening the fruitful autonomy of each level of government? We reply: by permanent consultation and co-ordination in all questions that invite Ottawa and the provinces to take joint action. It matters little whether this action arises from officially concurrent fields of jurisdiction-
I suppose such as agriculture and immigration.
[DOT]-or whether It is inspired by a newly discovered overlapping of interests; the essential aim is to develop within the federation a stable and flexible method permitting the federal and provincial governments to act together, when they so wish, and for the common good. Obviously, this cooperation must be agreed to freely; for co-operative federalism affords no place to coercion.
I cite that particularly because as far as we can determine this new training plan was handed to the provinces as the result of an arbitrary decision, not one reached after cooperation between the federal government and the provincial governments. With reference to the federal system and how the governments which make up the federal system should work to solve our problems and arrive at workable solutions to the problems which face the country, I wish to quote again from one of the many speeches on co-operative federalism made by Mr. Favreau. This speech was made on May 4, 1964, to the Canadian Club, Montreal.

speechtext:
I do not have any difficulty in relating these remarks to the bill. When speakers from the various parties were making their comments on the bill last night they mentioned several times the arbitrary fashion in which the decision was taken by the federal government to withdraw from direct financial support of education and to scrap the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act. I believe my remarks are related to the bill because I am complaining about the fact that the decision to undertake this program was a unilateral one and not in keeping with the policy which has been expressed so frequently in the past by various spokesmen for the government. I should like to hear from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources before this debate is completed to ascertain if he can make any sense out of the many things he has been saying over the years about co-operation with the provinces. How can he accept the type of action which we have before us?
This measure, Mr. Speaker, does involve the provinces. The measure it is replacing, the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act, involved the provinces. I am talking about methods which the two levels of government in Canada should use to bring about the best type of co-operation in order to evolve workable plans for the implementation of particular policies. I believe, therefore, that to this extent these remarks are relevant.
However, the point is that what the government is embarking upon now represents a very sharp change from the policy of the past few years of co-operating with the provinces in joint schemes. If a province did not want to have the federal government in a particular field, provision was made for that province to opt out. It seems to me that was not a bad policy in a complex country such as Canada where we have to make all sorts of compromises. Now, however, we have gone back to what hon. Mr. Favreau called the classical way of operating a federal system. The federal government says, you look after your affairs and we will look after ours; we will keep them separate as much as possible. It seems to me that in 1967 we cannot operate in this way. Certainly we cannot operate in this way in the fields of education and manpower because people are mobile. They move from one province to another, so this type of action goes against our whole industrial structure.
April 25, 1967

The decision has been made by the government not to be involved in education as they define education. They are going to be involved in retraining. The bill contains some points which I think are good. The level of payments to be made is certainly better than the level of payments made to those receiving unemployment insurance benefits. It would certainly pay a person to undergo retraining rather than to be unemployed. While I am on that subject, I believe that the unemployment insurance benefits have been in need of revision for some time. No one will get rich under this scheme but at least he will be better off than he was in the past.
In addition, I like the provision that a person does not have to be unemployed in order to qualify for retraining under this new measure. A person could be employed at a low level job which did not suit him and if he had the ability he could be referred for retraining and receive an allowance for his expenses. This is a good feature.
There are a number of weaknesses in the bill. I believe that many of them result from the fact that the kind of consultation to which I was referring a few minutes ago did not take place or was limited to consultation with provincial authorities. I have made it my business to talk with people who are involved in retraining and adult education in the major metropolitan centres of Canada. These people have not been consulted. These are the people who are daily working in the field. They know what the problems are, how you organize a course, who should be admitted to the course, how many instructors are available to teach these courses. As far as I can determine the bill was drawn up by people in Ottawa, undoubtedly very well qualified and well educated, who have had no actual experience in the field of retraining and adult education. I can say this with certainty because I have been speaking to the people concerned in the major cities of Canada and they were not consulted. It seems to me if they had been consulted many of the questions and problems which are being raised now could have been avoided. I am going to raise some of these problems later.
I am going to pose some questions, and I imagine the minister will be answering later so his staff may wish to take note of them. The first one is, what is the role of the universities? Are they able to contract directly with the federal department to provide training? I mention this because it is important. Universities are more and more becoming 23033-967
Occupational Training
creatures of the provincial governments. This position flows from the decisions taken last fall. If they can only provide training contracted with the provincial government's approval, this further reduces their capabilities for independent educational action.
The second question is, what is the intention of the manpower department with respect to holding clients who are eligible for training and allowances but for whom a particular course may not start for two weeks, a month or possibly six weeks? What happens to them during the interval? The local authorities, whether they be provincial or municipal, who provide some courses will have to have time to organize the courses and find teachers. What do they do with these people during that period? Are they on allowances or unemployment insurance benefits during that interval?
Since many people would find part time training better suited to their needs, why has provision not been made for the cost of part time training, including part time allowances? In one city I know that more than half of the people entering the adult education program were people who were taking night school training. They were not asking to leave their jobs to go on full time allowances, but they were taking this form of training to improve their standing. The people who attend evening classes are not concerned about the question of allowances, but will the bill permit their tuition fees to be paid?
There are other possibilities that could be considered here. It might be that some people could work half a day and attend courses for half a day. Is there any provision in the bill for allowances to be paid on a pro rata basis in that type of situation? In the large cities such as Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and Winnipeg, you will find a large number of people in this category. In order to function at all well, a local manpower office operating under this new measure will have to have access to the most up to date and comprehensive information about training and upgrading throughout the country. What provision is being made to accumulate and continuously process this kind of information since at present it is not available anywhere in Canada?
The task of accumulating this information, it seems to me, will be tremendous. Undoubtedly some of it is available at certain levels in the adult education departments but it will take quite some time for the departments themselves to gather the necessary

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
background information. The provision of an adequate information service to support the manpower training program will cost a great deal. The estimates of the manpower department do not appear to include any such major items. Are we then to conclude that the manpower department is expected to function without the provinces or adequate information services? In so far as the budget is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I really do not know how the department is going to operate this rather ambitious program next year with the amount of money shown in the estimates at the present time.
Why does the bill specify that research costs must be shareable with the provinces? Should there not be substantial sums available for contracting research directly from various agencies in addition to such research as naturally involves provincial governments, departments of education and so on?
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Another question is: Is it not true that the implication of this bill is that the least qualified people in society will be turned on to the labour market for a one to three year period? I am thinking particularly of the youngster who leaves school at the age of 16 or 17, the type previously referred to as a drop-out. At the present time he can enrol at a vocational school and receive training right away.
I realize that the answer has already been suggested by somebody, namely, that the province can pay for that. But I do not think that this is a good way to operate. If this same person gets married after one year and then has a dependant, he immediately becomes eligible for training under this bill. Therefore it seems to me that there are certain discriminations and inconsistencies here which really do not hold up very well.
Another question which comes to mind is whether there has been any consultation between the department of manpower and officials of ARDA. ARDA is concerning itself with education in certain depressed regions of the country. I rather like the ARDA approach; they are concerned with the social aspects as well as the economic. I have the feeling that the attitude of the department of manpower is a direct result of the report of the Economic Council and is perhaps too much economics-oriented without taking into account social aspects.
However, I should like to ask what co-operation or discussion has taken place with ARDA officials, who as I say are involving themselves in education and retraining in certain

areas of Canada. The previous speaker, the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Keays), mentioned that there are too many cases where one department of government does not know what another department is doing.
I have said that there are some good aspects to this new bill. I have also made certain criticisms of it. However, I think it is a great shame that the government is taking an altogether different approach from that taken under the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act. That act did not meet with very much opposition from the provinces of Canada. Certainly there was a federal involvement in the field of education or technical and vocational training, or whatever you want to call it, but there was no great objection to that and the act worked quite well. There were certain faults. People had to be unemployed to qualify under that act. However, it seems to me that if that act had been retained and amended to bring in some of the good features in this bill we would have been much farther ahead.
It seems to me that this bill has been designed to meet particular doctrines or policies that the government has adopted. Very often in the past we in this party have been accused of being doctrinaire. It seems to me that this may be said of the government at the present time. They have said that they will have nothing to do with education as they define it, which seems to me a very doctrinaire approach, certainly not the kind of approach that will solve the problems of a modern industrial society with a mobile population.
The majority of the provinces of Canada had no objection to the type of operation that we had in the past to give federal assistance to education. There were some objections from the province of Quebec, and this sort of thing was handled by opting out provisions and by making money grants available. I do not know why we cannot continue in that way. To me this bill is a move in the wrong direction.
I should now like to say a few words about the staffing of the department, I know that the intention is to make it a prestige department, to recruit university graduates, bright, able people, and to give the department a good salary level. At one time the government was talking about trying to make the department a prestige department like finance or external affairs. That is fine. I think the stigma which attached to the unemployment insurance offices in the past was undesirable,
April 25, 1967

and anything we can do to raise the prestige of the manpower department is all to the good.
An active recruiting campaign is now on to attract able people to the department to be the counsellors. However, the job of counselling is a very important one and it seems to me it can only be done well by people who have lived for some time and have gained some experience. The person who is newly out of university or who has very few years of experience is not going to be an effective counsellor for quite some time. True, you should hire them and use them in subordinate jobs. But the type of people who should do the counselling of the people who need retraining should be mature adults with a number of years of experience and living behind them.
It occurs to me that this type of person does exist in many of our cities across the country. I think, for example, of people employed by school boards and boards of education. I hope some method can be worked out among local manpower centres whereby the staffs of the manpower centres, many of whom will be new and inexperienced, can rely on the experience which has been gained by these other people I have just mentioned.
There is one other point in connection with counselling that I wonder about, and again I raise it in the form of a question. I believe there are to be five regional directors across the country who will have very great powers. They will have a great deal of discretion in decision making. They are to decide who should take re-training and who should not. One would therefore hope that different criteria do not apply in different parts of the country but that a plan will be worked out so that some common denominator applies. I say this because people could be admitted for training in one part of the country because of the attitude of the particular regional director and his staff but the same people would not be admitted in other parts of the country because other centres operated under different criteria and arrived at different decisions.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have noted that other speakers in this debate have, like myself, raised a great many questions, and rightly so. This is a most important measure and I hope that the staff have been taking note of these questions. I would inform the minister that we will want to hear answers to these questions either before second reading or in committee before this measure finally goes through.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very unfortunate that this very important bill follows so closely on the heels of the unification bill which has just been passed this afternoon because long after the arguments which have been presented during the last two or three weeks have been forgotten the effect of the bill will be with us. The beneficial results of this bill, if properly applied, will mark the minister as one of our great ministers and, as you know, I do not say that lightly.
This is a bill which deals with individuals, not with groups. It deals with the individual's rights, his apprehensions and fears, and indeed with whether or not the individual Canadian is going to be able to make a living. As time progresses and these awesome changes in technology take place from day to day, it is all very well to say to a welder, for example: "We have just developed a brand new machine and instead of you standing over a piece of steel for days on end you will just have to put it into this machine and it will weld it for you". That is fine. The great benefits of automation are not realized by workmen who think their jobs are in jeopardy. The workman fears the new technology and fears the way it will disrupt his life. He resists change. This bill attempts to alleviate his fears by saying: "Look, you need not worry. You will survive and enter new employment fields. We have stafE and research facilities behind us and we shall make sure that your training will benefit you and the nation."
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
That there will be many difficulties connected with this measure is true. I submit that its success depends on those clauses of the bill having to do with research. I am amazed sometimes at how slow educators, technicians and tutors are to accept the realities of the moment. Let me give an example. I have had 18 to 20 years experience in the construction field. Under a program similar to this one vocational schools are training plasterers although plastering as a trade is dying. In other words, when the student has finished his course there will not be a job for him. The same might apply to carpenters, plumbers, and electricians.
In the construction field we need installers and assemblers, but difficulties are created because one group of tradesmen instals windows, another group instals kitchen cabinets, another instals plumbing, another instals

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
doors, and so on. A great change is contemplated in clause 10 of the bill which will provide for real research in the field of technology. If the government assembles a competent research staff I am sure that adults taking the courses will benefit greatly.
It must be remembered, nevertheless, that we are dealing with human beings. It is all very well for counsellors to say, "You ought to be retrained because your trade is vanishing", but the applicant's feelings as a human being must be considered. In this regard the government ought to co-operate with management which, contrary to popular assumption, is willing to co-operate in this field.
It must be remembered too that when a man retrains for a job his living standard drops by about 25 per cent. Tradesmen retraining are willing to put up with hardships. Nevertheless it is difficult, having qualified for a trade and worked at it for 10 or 15 years, to be told that the old skills must be forgotten and that new skills must be learned.
Nothing is as valuable to management as an old, experienced employee. Such employees are loyal, they know the work and they are a very real asset. I am an employer and I should be only too happy to pay tradesmen seeking retraining $10, $15 or $20 to keep their services. One man has been with me for a long time and I should like to keep him. I should like to see the government co-operating with management much more than it has in the past. In fact, I think that management will co-operate more readily than will the provinces.
That brings me to my second point. During his remarks the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) said that we have lost sight of co-operative federalism. I say, of course, that nothing will be more conducive to co-operation than this measure. It is senseless arguing that education is of local or provincial jurisdiction. On a man's education depends his standard of living. On the education of the labour force will depend such things as national unemployment or employment, the increase or decrease of production, the fall or rise of our balance of payments and whether the national economy prospers or falters. The provinces jealously guard their jurisdiction in the field of education. Their jurisdiction is concerned with individuals. Do the provinces say when unemployment strikes: "Fine, we will look after the unemployed in our provinces?" I submit they do not. Unemployment remains a federal responsibility and it ought not to be argued
{Mr. Otto.]
that education, especially adult education, should not be a federal responsibility.
The British North America Act, one of the loosest constitutions in existence can be interpreted in almost any way one wishes. I suggest that the British North America Act applies best to the government that is quickest to take the initiative. I doubt that the people of Canada would support the argument of the provinces that education ought to be within provincial jurisdiction. Indeed, I am quite sure that all Canadians would be willing to have education under federal jurisdiction. This bill will only succeed in its aims if the minister insists that its subject matter comes within federal jurisdiction, with the senior level of government assuming the responsibility for payment as well as responsibility for administering the legislation.
It is incorrect to think that the Canadian people will not support the idea that adult education should come under federal jurisdiction completely. Some imagine that in this country we have two groups of taxpayers, one supporting provincial governments and the other supporting the federal government. That is not so. The same taxpayers support the federal and provincial governments and pay taxes to both levels. The tax revenue of the country still comes from the country's taxpayers. If we recognize that matters such as the economy, unemployment and productivity are of national concern we should recognize that education, especially adult education, ought to be within the national jurisdiction.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
A further point I should like to raise concerns unemployment insurance. I realize this is touched on briefly in the bill before us and I am in support of the clause which deals with it. At the same time it must be remembered that if we are to expect Canadians to take advantage of facilities for adult education it will be necessary to convince them that they will not suffer undue financial hardship as a result. It is not likely that Canadians will be willing to lower their standard of living to an appreciable extent merely because through no fault of their own their jobs have disappeared. So we must arrange these payments in such a way that a man will receive not less than 75 per cent of his former earnings while he is retraining.
This a matter which ought to be taken out of the municipal field because the municipalities are governed largely by a group elected

by the establishment. Similarly, the provincial governments are in effect representative of the establishment. On the other hand, we in this house represent the disestablished, and it is the disestablished who must take advantage of this bill.
The minister should pursue the course he has set himself with strength and vigour. I am sure the consequences of this measure will be rewarding if its terms are put into effect stringently, vigorously and with some thought for the future.

I wanted to say that I feel this bill would have received more meaningful consideration by parliament had it gone before one of the committees of parliament before this debate began. No matter what one may think of the unification bill, the transport bill or the Bank Act, each of these measures is in its own way the better because the opportunity was taken to examine it carefully in a committee of parliament.
I myself feel in some need of adult retraining in this very sphere. I recognize that the minister and the government are captives of the parliamentary timetable. Because of the demands of this timetable they may be in danger of asking parliament to enact legislation which has not received sufficiently thorough examination by members of parliament or by the provincial governments.
I do not intend to speak for very long. I am sympathetic toward the basic objectives of this legislation. But if I were ever to ask the Canada Council to give me a grant I think I would ask that I be allowed to conduct a study in the use of what I call irony, a study of the use made by governments, by ministers, by all of us, of what might be called ironical defences of what we propose to do. I think that the subject of manpower retraining would be a good place to start. If I wanted somebody to come to my defence-because on a number of occasions I tend to be open-minded-I would choose as a supporter of my views none other than the distinguished chancellor of Queen's University who has had some interesting things to say about the constitutional position vis-a-vis education.
I was interested, as I suppose all of us should be, in the government's about-face last
Occupational Training
October, its retreat from concern with assistance to higher education. At the time of that retreat it made an advance in a related field, and this legislation is obviously part of that advance. The irony on which I like to reflect is that we can find a neat constitutional excuse for enacting this bill at the very time we are finding a constitutional excuse for withdrawing from a field which I feel is of equal importance and concern to the government of Canada, that is, the field of higher education. Perhaps my council grant would run out if this were the only evidence I could bring to bear on the use of irony. But why can we not be frank with the people of Canada once in a while?
I also wish to express regret that I have had no opportunity to study the letters from various provincial jurisdictions expressing the concern they feel about the working out of the formula for manpower retraining. This is despite the fact that the minister kindly promised to table them. I have had to rely on newspaper accounts which are not the best evidence, I admit. Apparently the reporters are able to see mail which members of parliament up to now at any rate have not had the opportunity to study. As I say, the minister did agree to the tabling of these letters subject to the consent of the provinces concerned. I make no charge, no criticism. I presume that some at least of the provinces have not yet agreed to the tabling of the correspondence. Apparently, though the province of Ontario has done so, because in the Globe and Mail of April 22 there is a fairly extensive article entitled "Queens' Park Points A Finger At Ottawa". The subheading reads: "The Retraining Row". Far be it from me to feel under any obligation to present a case for the province of Ontario, but it is my impression-the minister may correct me if I am mistaken-that there is a very genuine concern felt about this legislation, not just a timid reaction but a genuine concern among all the provinces save two. This arises, if my information is correct, from a feeling there has been insufficient consideration of the regulations and of the effect of this new concept.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I share several of the views expressed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) as to the working of the ARDA program. I have been following the developments in northeastern New Brunswick with a great deal of interest. Of course anybody who represents any part of that province knows of

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
the drastic need for an ARDA program, in fact for adult education and a thorough-going upgrading of the economic and social life in that part of New Brunswick. But I hope, as did the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, that the manpower retraining program will be dovetailed with the ARDA program and that the human and social needs of the people will be the prime consideration.
I have an idea that the minister has a very genuine feeling for human problems. This has been demonstrated in other areas of his departmental concern, particularly in the very much improved immigration procedures that he announced. By the way, Mr. Speaker, I think that announcement shows the benefit of a parliamentary committee's thoughtful consideration of a program, and had a parliamentary committee had the opportunity to examine this bill I think it would have been so much the better for it.
I also hope there will be a close tie-in of this program with the developing facilities for educational television. That also needs thorough research and examination by parliament. We shall have other opportunities to speak on this aspect, but may I just say I hope ARDA will be tied in with manpower retraining and that those who are administering this bill when it has been passed by parliament will not forget the advantages of educational television.
To return for a second to my feeling about the use of the word irony, may I quote a comment made by Dr. Corry in what I think was a very important speech which he made On October 26, 1966, to the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada. As hon. members will recall, the government staked out the federal role in cultural matters, manpower training and research in its public announcement about the same time last October, or in early November. Dr. Corry had some comments to make that I think are relevant to this bill and to a consideration of what I might with great respect say was the over-simplified view of the constitutional aspects of education given to us by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto). If it were as simple as the hon. member suggested I am sure the minister, as spokesman for the province of Quebec in the federal cabinet, would feel that a good many of his worries were over.
Dr. Corry said:
In a number of quarters we are being warned that the very existence of our country depends on vastly more Canadians becoming bilingual- *in essence, acquiring some facility in French as
[Mr. Fairweather.l
well as English. Without judging this contention but allowing that it may well be so, could we count on nine English speaking provinces grasping this urgency and making the necessary educational provision? Would the sum of these efforts add up to enough? Is it not clear that there may well be the need for emphasis, support, and direction being provided by the government of Canada?
This is the key question that Dr. Corry asked:
Is it not strange that numbers of those who warn us of the critical nature of bilingual needs should in almost the same breath be saying that the government of Canada has no role to play in education?
But, it will be asked, does not section 93 of the British North America Act give exclusive power over education to the provinces? This is correct, subject to a limitation that is likely to become more portentous as time goes on. Literally, the words of section 93 are "In and for each province, the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education."
If there are national needs and objectives that require concerted educational policy in two, several, or all provinces, no provincial legislature is by itself competent in the matter, and judicial interpretation on other comparable aspects of the distribution of powers under the British North America Act makes it clear that parliament is competent, under "the peace order and good government" clause.
It must be on this ground that Prime Minister Pearson, in his proposal to the federal-provincial conference now meeting-*
This speech, of course, was made, as I have said, last October 26.
-asserted federal jurisdiction in the training and retraining of adults for participation in the labour force. It is to be hoped that a reading of this particular assertion along with other general disclaimers in the text of his proposal about federal authority in education will not give rise to inferences that the federal government has neither status nor lively concern in the education of highly skilled and highly educated manpower in the universities.
May I interpolate here that this is the point I want to make in my few remarks on this stage of the bill. Fine, go ahead with the manpower retraining program with basic enthusiasm for its objectives, but do not in the same policy announcement, so to speak, and in the same area of vital national concern ignore the need for highly educated specialists coming from the universities. To return to the speech made by Dr. Corry.
It would be incongruous to be asserting federal authority over training for run-of-the-mill jobs in the labour force and abandoning it totally for all professional, scientific, and technical personnel educated by the universities. It is the latter who will be critical for national objectives in the future.
. .. The federal government is attempting to make clear it has a constitutional responsibility for adult
April 25, 1967

retraining programs, research, and cultural development, and that these are not, constitutionally speaking, educational matters falling within the jurisdieiton of the provinces, from which the federal authority is excluded.
I hope I have an opportunity before very long, perhaps arising out of the speech from the throne in the next session, if there is any next session for those of us who have been waiting for it for a little while, to be able to support enthusiastically a vigorous program Of financial help for the very areas of highly skilled people in another aspect of Canadian need that has been so clearly set out by Dr. Corry.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I feel that this bill would have been better had we had the opportunity to examine it in a committee. I had hoped to have an opportunity to study or take into consideration the serious doubts about the mechanics of this legislation as carried out by the provinces. Unfortunately that is not to be. May I also re-echo the plea made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond that this new program not be isolated from those projects envisaged by the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. Lastly, I hope that the as yet untapped area, untapped in Canada but used to a particular effect in Italy, of educational television will not be neglected when the minister goes about establishing this new policy.
