Mr. Speaker, it did not take me half a day, like the minister, to set the record straight. It took him half a day to make charges such as those I have just mentioned, whereas it took me barely two minutes to make a correction.
Once again, I apologize to the minister for disturbing him while he is reading the newspapers but, you know how it is, Mr. Speaker, I have electors to represent here and I will do it to the best of my ability.
I, therefore, come back to the bill dealing with occupational training as I understand it.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation as introduced in Bill No. C-278 is one that enables everybody to evade their responsibilities.
As far as providing our people with the means and the opportunity to secure a more advanced occupational and technical training, I am all for it. But I am not so sure about the means that are being suggested. To support this, let me refer to the answers the minister himself gave to certain questions we put to him when we asked: How is it that so many Quebec people cannot follow the occupational training courses? And the federal Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) replied: It is because the province of Quebec lacks the necessary facilities to enable the unemployed to follow these training courses.
So, if all our citizens who need them do not follow the occupational training courses this year, next year or two years from now, the

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
minister will simply rise and say: It is not our fault if the provinces lack the facilities. We are ready to pay the provinces if they provide the facilities. Yes, we will pay the provinces, but if they lack the facilities, that is not our fault. And the minister can quietly sit down and say: I have done my duty; I have introduced legislation that does not apply to everyone because the provinces lack the required facilities. And he can blame the provinces and the minister can continue to read his newspapers in peace.
But if people vote as they are doing now against legislation that is not implemented as it should be, the minister will call them young punks, and to those who feel that things are not going fast enough, the minister will say, as he is wont to say in his rigmarole, that they are irresponsible. The minister will also say: If we only had members who would stay put and keep quiet! He will go to their constituencies and say: Elect a Conservative, a Liberal, or a "caille". As far as he is concerned, it is all the same thing provided they stay put. That is the first requirement. And the minister will say:	I put legislation
through. It is not my fault if other governments cannot do any better. It is never the fault of any given government, but always somebody else's fault.
It is the way the minister has been answering. When he is asked: How is it that our labourers who need retraining cannot take this training because they are refused in the manpower centres in our ridings? The minister says: It is not our fault, it is the fault of the provinces that are lacking in facilities. This bill enables all concerned to evade their responsibilities or to pass the buck. Then he can sit down saying: I put legislation through. Some people talk too much while it was being considered, but it was finally passed. If it does not operate as it should, well, it is not our fault, it is somebody else's fault.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation, as drafted now in Bill No. C-278 cannot have any other effects. It is the system which is wrong. When there is an objective to achieve, when we want to assist some groups of people, we always have to involve two governments in the deal, and two governments which interfere with each other, two governments which have administrative expenses, whose functions overlap and where no effort is being made on one side or the other to make the legislation operative, because when things do not operate as they should, or successfully,

one just has to fold one's arms and say: It is the other government's fault.
That is what this legislation has again in store for us. I would not want the minister to think that I am opposed to adult occupational training. The minister cannot detect in anything which I say now the slightest opposition to adult occupational training or to retraining of those who have been displaced on account of automation or modern production technology. No, that is not the case.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
On the contrary, I would like to see an act like this one-there are good things in it-to be really applicable, without loopholes, one that does not allow the blame to be put on someone else, one that assigns responsibilities in such a way that, if it fails to operate, we can point a finger at one government, and not two, and say: You are to blame if things are not working out; and do not try to put the blame on another government.
Mr. Speaker, once again, even if the matter is as vital, important, and necessary as the training of adults, because many individuals are still being displaced by automation and modern techniques, implementation of the act is entrusted to two different governments, two different organizations, two bureaucracies, and consequently causes double expense.
It is the individual displaced by automation, for instance, or the man employed in an industry where technical changes are expected to take place who will want to take those occupational training courses and he will apply first to the manpower centre, a federal institution.
You will note the intricacies of this administrative process. This federal manpower centre will have to turn to provincial organizations and administrations to know about the opportunities and facilities for receiving such or such individual; and then, that will fall back into the hands of the provincial authority.
The provincial authority will report on such opportunities to the federal manpower centre and this centre will return the individual involved, like a football thrown from hand to hand, to the provincial occupational training institutions. When the time comes to pay for the courses, the federal centre will pay the provincial centre, and when the time comes to pay the living allowances, again the federal government will pay the individual. And there will always be overlapping. That individual will be sent for retraining-he will practically be sent on a bicycle-from the
April 25, 1967

federal to the provincial government so that the individual will always be caught between two governments, two administration centres.
We will have to pay taxes to cover the administration costs of the federal manpower centre, we will have to pay more taxes to the provincial government to support the administration and pay the cost of the paperwork and the provincial bureaucrats who will look after this individual, and there will always be duplication in administrative and bureaucratic expenditures.
The poor Quebeckers will have to deal with two ministers, two deputy ministers, federal and provincial bureaucrats and auditors; they will have to foot two expense accounts and will also have to pay taxes twice to cover administrative expenses, once to the federal government and again to the provincial government.
This is absolutely abnormal, Mr. Chairman. This is another proof that our system is basically wrong, since each time we want to pass legislation in the interest of an individual, of a group of individuals, or of a class of people, two governments must deal with it instead of one.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill No. C-278, is another intrusion by the federal government into a field which is not its own, the educational field. And this is not the first intrusion by the federal government into the field of education.
I can well remember that my hon. colleague, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), has written a little booklet that everybody should read, giving a detailed account of all the intrusions by the federal government. But we are concerned here with the retraining of manpower, and even if the present intrusion by the federal government, into the occupational training field will not prevent directly the provincial government from setting up an over-all plan for the retraining and training of citizens, whether they are students, teenagers or adults, it will nevertheless prevent the establishment of an over-all program controlled by a single authority in the educational field, so as to provide a link between the training of young people and their further training, once they have become adults, in order to cope with the never-ending technological changes.
There will be no overall plan, but two separate programs, one for secondary education and one for adult education. As a result, it will be impossible to establish an overall system which would co-ordinate education in 23033-968
Occupational Training
Canada at all levels, enabling people continually to adjust to evolution, modern technology and automation.
Let us take another example concerning refresher courses under the Adult Occupational Training Act. Let us take the case of a grade 10 school teacher who has a diploma from a teachers' college. Would not modern progress require, Mr. Speaker, that after some five years' teaching experience this man take a one-year sabbatical leave to see how grade 10 is taught in other schools, or else, return to other specialized schools, to learn new pedagogical developments and new teaching methods for grade 10 teachers.
I see that the minister nods his head. It is precisely there that the federal government takes charge of this grade 10 teacher who wants to improve his education for one year. This, in my opinion, has two serious shortcomings; first, a teacher is taken away from a provincial system of education to be placed for one year under the authority of the federal Department of Manpower and Immigration. And then, is this not also intended to prevent a single authority in matters of education, that is the provincial authority, from looking after the further training of such a teacher who, after teaching for five years, seeks to improve himself?
Such a measure will, in effect, make a clean break, because it will bewilder such a teacher seeking occupational training as an adult, after having taught for five years. To improve himself, he will have to come under the federal Minister of Manpower and Immigration.
In view of what the minister has told us, he will probably be given newspapers, in order to teach him to read the papers. That is the way our school teachers will be trained.
Mr. Speaker, this is a clear case of intrusion by the federal government. I have only referred to two points, because the time available will not permit me to explain further, but I shall have the opportunity to refer to this again.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I shall have an opportunity to come back to them but, first of all and to sum up, they prevent the establishment of a general plan to co-ordinate the whole training of the citizen, whether it be during his technical, secondary or university studies, relating all these elements to his occupational training as an adult; the intrusion of the federal government makes here a clear break in the whole scheme that could be built around the Quebec citizen or the Canadian citizen.

April 25, 1367
Occupational Training
It also prevents the formulation of a general plan for refresher courses, as I mentioned a moment ago, taking as an example school teachers who could, every five years, refresh or improve their knowledge either by seeing what is being done elsewhere, or by learning more modern teaching methods, for these also change every year.
Mr. Speaker, as far as work itself is concerned, this is also an intrusion by the federal government, since it prevents those who are empowered to act and who are responsible in this field, that is the provincial authorities, from setting up a comprehensive program so as to provide for a reduction of working hours, which is in keeping with the times. In the Express magazine, a French periodical, an article was published on April 22, I believe, saying that an American company, after a study based upon modern processing methods and computer operations, had established that in 30 years from now, the average working week would be about 24 hours.
Well, the authorities could draw up a comprehensive plan combining a reduction of the worker's time on the job and an increase in the time he must spend to complete an adult occupational training course in step with automation and modern production techniques.
This also, Mr. Speaker, comes under the provincial authority, but the program set forth today will prevent the development of such comprehensive plan by the authorities who have the jurisdiction in that field, to wit: the provincial authorities.
Mr. Speaker, I am not against-and I wish to point it out once more-a legislation concerning the occupational training of adults. I think that the legislation has very good points and I should not like it to be dropped merely on account of the basic matters which I have listed. Moreover, I do not want the citizens of Quebec to be deprived thereof, because a minister has deemed it advisable to bring down mixed legislation based on federal and provincial authorities, enabling each authority to back out of their responsibilities while holding the other responsible if the legislation does not operate successfully.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, instead of taking direct objection to this bill, I would rather move an amendment, because although in my opinion the bill, as drafted, could be greatly useful, I believe that the amendment I intend to move now, on second reading can be of greater service still.

My amendment is as follows:
I move, seconded by my good friend the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), to whom I am thankful because he shares these opinions as he is not a "caille", as the Minister of Manpower and Immigration says, but one of those who prefer to speak up even if it should prevent the minister from reading his papers, that all the words after the world "that" be deleted and replaced by the following:
This house, while of the opinion that all necessary steps must be taken to ensure that proper occupational training is available to every adult Canadian citizen who needs it, also believes nonetheless that no legislation providing occupational training for adults would be sufficient unless it provided also a system of fiscal compensation for any province wanting to set up its own program of occupational training for adults.
Mr. Speaker, I could let you read the
amendment to the house and continue my remarks afterwards.

I wish to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that if you have any doubts about this amendment, whether it is in order or legal, I could give you the reasons in favour thereof.
The purpose of the amendment is to improve this piece of legislation. You may note that I am not saying this is a bad bill; in the contrary, I think that any piece of
April 25, 1967

legislation which is intended to improve the occupational training of adults should be considered seriously and that we should try to legislate to that effect.
Now, my amendment will enable the provinces wishing to do so to entrust the federal government with the occupational training of adults.
Nothing will prevent Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland or even Quebec from waiving their authority in favour of the federal government. Nothing will prevent them from doing so, under that amendment.
On the other hand, those provinces that will wish to legislate in that field, to have their own legislation regarding the occupational training of adults will be able to do so, under the amendment.
Those provinces wishing to take advantage of that amendment will be wholly responsible for the occupational training of adults. Then, not one member from Quebec will be justified in rising and asking what the minister is doing? As a matter of fact, he could say since the province insisted on being solely responsible, it must therefore assume its responsibilities.
Then, if a member rises in the provincial legislature and asks what the minister is doing, it will not be possible for that provincial minister to reply: It is the fault of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration who reads newspapers. He could say: It is my fault, since I am wholly responsible in the field of occupational training of adults.
The minister will find that, by the same token, if some provinces take advantage of that amendment, he will no longer have to say: It is not my fault, it is the provinces' fault. And he will be able to keep on reading his papers.
Mr. Speaker, such is the purpose of the amendment: to ensure that provincial jurisdiction is not infringed and that the provinces may establish their own occupational training program for adults; to see that, with this adult occupational training program, other larger over-all plans may be generated within those provinces such as, for instance the co-ordination and education of young people with that of adults. That is the improvement wished by those who not only have to face modern technology or automation but who wish to improve in other fields such as, for instance, in the teaching profession.
Occupational Training
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The provinces will be allowed to operate other over-all plans if they take advantage of the amendment. They could, for instance, combine the reductions in working hours and the increase in hours devoted to adult training.
Mr. Speaker, I move this amendment in the hope that everyone will realize that it is an improvement over the legislation before us at this time. Without taking anything away from the legislation, it represents an improvement which I hope the minister will accept, because it will not take anything away from it.
The amendment means simply that the provinces wishing and feeling able to do so could initiate their own occupational training plan. Then, the provinces will benefit from tax equalization, which means that the federal government will give back to them, in the form of tax equalization, what it would cost to implement that system in a given province.
For instance, should the plan be applied in Quebec, the federal government would cease to collect an equal amount in taxes and the Quebec government could thus benefit from that amount which the federal government would refrain from collecting, that is an amount equal to the cost to the federal government of implementation of the plan. *
Mr. Speaker, under those circumstances the province collecting the taxes would implement its own plan according to the specific aims of the province. That would spare double administrative costs, and that is very important. In fact, we would no longer need to pay officials in Ottawa and Quebec city to implement the same bill. One single group of examiners, inspectors and bureaucrats would be enough. Instead of paying officials twice, we would pay them only once. Instead of paying a federal and a provincial inspector to check whether a building designed for occupational training of adults has actually been built according to standards, only one would be paid, and thus money would be saved.
Instead of paying two architects, one provincial and one federal, to supervise the works, only one would be paid. Instead of two accounting systems to ascertain whether an adult taking occupational training has received his school allowance or his moving expenses, we would have only one control system, and thus significant savings could be realized.
23033-968J

April 25. 1967
Occupational Training
On the other hand, the provincial authorities could provide the adults with a much better occupational training system than the one suggested by the minister, on account of the savings effected in the administrative field, for there would be only one single authority to operate and administer.
That causes delays and involves halfmeasures. The federal government may say: We want this to be done in such a way, while the provincial authorities will say: We want it this way. Finally, nothing will be done.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe the amendment I move today will improve the bill and enable the provinces to exercise their jurisdiction and their authority as far as education and labour legislation are concerned, since tax equalization will provide them with amounts of money equal to the expenditures brought about by the adult occupational training program.
Mr. Speaker, may I say that if you have any doubts as to whether or not this amendment is in order, I am prepared to put forward arguments to show that it is in order.

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien (for Mr. Marchand)
[Mr. Gregoire.l
for the second reading of Bill No. C-278, respecting the occupational training of adults.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH THE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to make some comments on this bill, Mr. Speaker, and to compliment the minister for bringing in a bill which certainly seems to have concern for the people as its major objective. This measure, of course, eliminates the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act which was introduced in 1960 by the then minister of labour in the Conservative government, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr). The need for education and re-education is something which nobody in this house denies today. We are in a world that from 1700 to 1900 amassed twice the knowledge it had previously, from 1900 to 1950 doubled that knowledge, and from 1950 to 1960 doubled it again. This is an amazing feat. Knowledge seems to spread. From 1960 to 1965 we doubled our knowledge again. I bring this point to your attention, Mr. Speaker, because it indicates that we have arrived at the stage of automation.
We find that a man who may have been fully trained in a skill or trade in 1960 is today looking for a new skill or trade. The job that he had may have been obliterated; it has gone into oblivion. We find that this situation applies to all of our courses of training. It is an axiom today that we train people to know more and more about less and less. When the need for a particular skill no longer exists we find that these people cannot turn to something else. They have to have retraining; they have to go back to school. This is one of the problems facing us today.
I feel we should take a good look at some of the things that have actually happened in Canada. In the year 1900 about 70 per cent of the people in Canada were engaged in farming. Today we find that less than 10 per cent of the people are engaged in this occupation. It is interesting to note that in those days the village blacksmith and the woodworker were the skilled mechanics, along with the man who ran the gristmill which turned the wheat into flour for making bread. These were the essential things in those days. Everyone was a skilled mechanic and was skilled in all the different phases of an operation whether it was making a wagon or whatever it might be.
Today we find that workmen play only a small part in the production of a machine. In other words, as I have said before, these skilled men know more and more about less and less. In the field of agriculture to which I
April 25, 1967

have referred, production efficiency has increased by over 50 per cent in the last ten years and is still increasing very rapidly as a result of the machines that have been produced. Last year, in fact, we were able to sell over a billion dollars worth of wheat to other countries. This situation was related to the mechanization and automation that have taken place over a period of years. Certainly this is increasing today by leaps and bounds. It is a fact of life that the training given today may be obsolete tomorrow. Therefore we need a training plan tailored to meet the problems created by automation.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
Although many people will qualify for retraining, some will not have the required academic education, and I am wondering what the minister plans for these people. In addition, what about those who are too old for training? Every week end I meet someone in this category. We have to exercise a little care and caution in the changing world of today. I met one fellow who was trained in one skill but had to be trained in another skill simply because his original skill was no longer required. Does the minister intend to keep offering retraining courses? In this event we will find ourselves on a merry-go-round.
I now want to talk about technical and vocational training schools. The Conservative government passed the former Technical and vocational training act in 1960 under the guidance of the minister of labour of that day, the hon. member for Ontario. Over $300 million was spent in a very short time on building schools. The Conservative government put up 75 per cent of the cost of construction and equipment. We are now going to move in another direction, and I should like to know where the money is coming from to construct the schools that will be required. We are going to have manpower centres but unless we have training schools it seems to me this bill is a backward step.
We also have those people who were trained in Salvation Army homes and institutions. These people have been doing a good job. I think all of us would agree that places like Concord have done a wonderful job. Young men from that institution have taken employment and have been very successful in their work. Are these people now to be cut off? I should like the minister to inform us on this.
Let us take the case of a boy of 17 going to high school who is either on any academic course or a vocational course. In the province
Occupational Training
of Ontario it is difficult to take any further course. Are these students to be cut off too? Why are they discriminated against? I see the minister shakes his head, but according to press reports this is exactly what has been happening. A report in the Globe and Mail for Saturday last had this to say:
Few of the 21,000 adults on job retraining in 54 communities in Ontario can afford to support themselves while attending full time classes.
Why are so many training-hungry adults facing the loss of educational opportunities at a time when Canada is so short of skilled manpower?
Part of the reason lies in good intentions on the part of new look federal cabinet minister Jean Marchand.
I would be the last to deny that the minister has good intentions. The article continues:
He wants to upgrade the nation's work force fast. But Ottawa is inexperienced at the education game and has been unwilling to listen to advice from the provinces.
In this regard I am wondering whether Premier Stanfield of Nova Scotia, Premier Robarts of Ontario and Premier Roblin of Manitoba were sufficiently consulted. I think it would be interesting to see the correspondence in this regard. It seems to me there is an allegation here that the minister has not looked into the question or consulted the provinces sufficiently. The article continues:
Another part lies in a liberal dose of what is described as bureaucratic arrogance by Ottawa, misunderstandings and some legislative bad luck.
I think the writer of the article is being very kind in his use of that last phrase. I bring this article to the attention of the minister as an indication that his public relations in this regard have not been very good. As I say, Mr. Speaker, I should like to see the correspondence that has been exchanged with respect to this plan. I do not think you can simply draw a line between the two as the minister has. I do not think there can be a black and a white in this regard.
When a student has completed an academic course of four years he does not want to loaf. He wants to go to work. He should come under the manpower training plan so he can finish his education in this field. In my opinion he has just as much right to manpower training as anybody else. I do not say this unkindly, but I submit that there are about 7,000 young people of Ontario who should not be placed in this position. Therefore I ask the minister to take another look at this question to see whether he can get together with the other provinces as well as my own province. Something must be done to ensure that these

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
young fellows du not become forgotten legions.
* I now want to dwell for a moment on what the minister proposes to do with the business 'colleges and trade schools. I would remind the minister, though he probably knows this better than I, that in high school two courses 'can be taken to grade 10 before going to business college. On the other hand, you can complete four years to grade 12 at high school and then go to business college. Usually these positions are taken by girls, though there are some men who attend. According to the figures I have before me, 44,641 people were trained in business schools.
: What is the position of the minister vis-avis the business colleges which are doing an excellent job? 1 was talking last night to some business colleagues who expressed the view that business colleges perform a very necessary function. They provide a finished training to equip people to go into business after a nine-month or six-month course following upon four years at high school.
Another point which I do not think has been sufficiently covered concerns trade 'schools. Last Saturday I was talking to a man who had employed a fellow who was trained at a trade school in Toronto, and he said that this boy was a dandy, that he does his job well and has other experience. Is the minister going to assist these people? I realize these schools are private concerns, but surely to goodness the minister does not think that good comes only from public enterprise. It has been proven over and over again that a complete education has great benefits. Over the years we have hired many stenographers and those who completed their education in the business schools have always been proficient and seemed to have a know-how to start with. I hope the minister will make certain that these people are trained and given allowances. If trainees come under program 5 there should be no discrimination because, after all, they are taxpayers of this country and are entitled to take private training if it is efficient.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I have grave doubts about the minister's bill with respect to its interfering with provincial affairs. I do not wish to say that the minister has been at fault; I think he is a nice fellow. But I do say that relations with the provincial premiers and ministers of education ought to have been better. Surely this whole matter could have been worked out before the introduction of the bill. There have
[Mr. Rynard.l
been arguments; at least, that is the impression left in my mind. Whether it is correct I do not know but I should be interested to read the correspondence to see whether my assumption is correct. Perhaps the provinces may be hard to get along with, but the minister knows how to deal with them. He is a smiling, diplomatic sort of fellow who has handled himself well in the house. Surely he could have done a better job in straightening out the many difficulties in which he finds himself.
I hope the minister will answer some questions on this important matter. As I have said before, the plan is a good one provided it works and provided the minister is willing to iron out problems with the provinces. In the over-all picture, with the rapidity of modern transport whereby people can move readily from Quebec to Ontario or Ontario to Quebec, from Quebec to British Columbia or to the maritimes, there ought to be national direction with respect to education. Under the British North America Act education is a provincial matter. It is easier to go from the maritimes to Vancouver by modern transportation facilities than it was to go from one village to another 100 years ago. With people able to move so easily from one province to another we ought to have some agreed national direction in education so that students will not lose time or become confused by reason of different textbooks and differently constituted classes.
I support the principle of the bill though I have many doubts about the minister's ability to carry through its intention. I wish the minister well and I hope he will provide some answers before we finish considering the bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH THE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin by saying that I feel Canadians almost everywhere appreciate the concept behind this bill. Many Canadians felt when the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) was appointed that this country was pioneering in certain respects. With automation spreading most Canadians thought that automation was indivisible and that the labour force would be indivisible. They felt that provincial boundaries meant nothing when mobility of labour and conditions of labour were taken into account. People from coast to coast felt that with the technical changes of automation provincial boundaries ought not to be a bar to technical training and mobility. Many of us feel that the minister has espoused much of this concept. Some of us
April 25, 1967

admire the way he has refused to permit questions of manpower and training to be pushed into provincial compartments entirely. The minister knows that these matters cannot be fenced off by provincial boundaries.
Some of us think of making this land into a single country one day with room for all our diversities, our two major cultures and languages, and so on. We hope that ways will constantly be developed whereby it will be possible for ideas of one sort or another to flow across provincial boundaries, in that way bringing about true unity within this country. One day we hope to see that unity. We do not go along with the nineteenth century idea of chopping this nation into ten divisions and saying that each division shall run everything as it sees fit.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH THE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

speechtext:
That sort of thinking will not turn us into one country and it is time that some of us said so. We want to make room for the diversities of this country and we want to give special status where special status is needed. We certainly do not accept the unrealistic concept of fencing everything off behind provincial boundaries. That can be done, but if it is done we shall not have a country.
I do not think that the hon. member on the other side who echoed this sentiment really agrees with what I am saying. I feel that his efforts do not make it easy for all Canadians to accept the diversity of our two major cultures. Let me say that I believe in diversity. I do not want to see everything reduced to a monolithic culture.

shall be completely unrealistic if we fail to face the facts of the twentieth century.

speechtext:
No
I am not on both sides of the fence. Because one or two provinces will not accept the facts of modern life is no reason for the other provinces to be held back by nineteenth century thinking when they need to be thinking in twentieth century terms.
I do not think there has been close enough co-operation between the federal government and the provinces in matters of manpower and manpower training. I know there have been difficulties for the minister and that he
Occupational Training
has been discouraged by certain actions. Nevertheless the minister must persevere and attempt to obtain a greater degree of co-operation than has been accorded him in the past.
In my hand I have a copy of the adult occupational training regulations, and I shall read regulation No. 14 under the heading of "General Regulations":
14. The minister may, at the request of the government of a province, join with that government in the establishment of a joint committee to assess manpower needs in that province.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
I realize that the minister has been cautious in case a province might not want him there to help assess manpower needs. But there is a halfway house. I do not see why in the world the minister should not approach a province in order to find out whether or not they would like his help in assessing manpower needs. That would be entirely different from sitting in Ottawa and saying: If you come to me maybe I will help you.
I assure the minister there are provinces which would welcome far closer co-operation than has been the case in the past. I know from past history that once they see programs going well in other provinces there are provincial governments which, even though they may have been backward in the initial stages, would be anxious to go along belatedly and say "Me, too".
The concept behind this bill is a good one and the measure itself contains many good features. However there are other features which are not so satisfactory, and it is because I am accepting and welcoming the principle of the bill that I wish to mention some of its shortcomings and deal with them briefly.
I believe this bill falls short in its treatment of the young people. At a time like the present in which formal schooling is being found wanting in so many ways and when there is great fluidity in our approach to this field, many young people are dropping out of school. Unfortunately many of them also drop out of society; a great many of them get lost. I was impressed by a phrase used earlier by one of the members of the official opposition. He said we needed more exit points in the educational system. This manpower training program ought to be providing some of these exit points. I do not wish the Minister to become involved in formal schooling or to infringe upon provincial rights, but when the provincial education systems have been unsuccessful in holding our young people, this training scheme should be there, ready and

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
waiting to take them in without keeping them waiting until they are one year older than the school leaving age.
In the Globe and Mail this morning I read that in the province of Ontario a great many North American Indians are leaving the schools long before they reach school leaving age. I have no doubt this applies to other provinces too. I am sure a program of training in manual and technical skills would be of great benefit to these young people. Very often those who are suited for academic training do not recognize that young people are thinking increasingly in terms of vocational and technical training-in terms of the skills necessary to look after the machines which are so important today. The minister of manpower should be prepared to step in when the school system cannot help these young people or provide them with the particular skills they need.
An hon. member who sits on my left said there was a real danger that this manpower training bill might encourage teen age marriages to a far greater extent than is desirable, since candidates have to be at least a year older than school leaving age and looking for work on the labour market.
Teen age marriages are undesirable in cases where there is no proper economic foundation for them. Under these proposals young people can qualify for training if they have a family to support. Otherwise they cannot. This is a situation which should be looked into.
I turn now to the shortcomings in which women are involved. As far as I understand this legislation, I see no provision with respect to childless widows. There are a great many childless widows in this country, women who have been left without support and who need training in order that they may earn a living. Many of them have no skill which would bring in a private income. A childless widow can be just as badly in need of a job as a widow with children. I should like to hear the minister explain how this gap in the legislation can be filled. It may be that his attention has not been drawn to this aspect. I know a great many people who belong in this category and who need a chance to retrain.
Again, if I read the regulations correctly, housewives are not considered to be members of the labour force-this is presumably when they are living at home-and therefore they are not considered eligible for training. I would point out that housework is certainly

labour, though unpaid labour. We never object very much in this country to women working; what we object to is women being paid. Housewives should have the right to train. They certainly have the right to go out and work now, because they are out in great numbers indeed. According to statistics published by the Department of Labour some time ago it is estimated that by 1970 half the married women of Canada will be gainfully employed outside their homes in the labour market. I believe that at present about one third of the labour force is composed of women. If they have the right to go out to work, they should have the right to retraining under these proposals.
I turn now to a more contentious subject. When we talk about assessing manpower needs it should not escape the attention of the government that one of the most pressing needs facing us at the present time is an assessment of the place of women in the labour market and the training of women for the work force. I am thinking now in terms of the women who can qualify for training under this legislation-women with dependants such as children of school age. We do not know how many of these there are across Canada.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
In 1965 there were 2 million women in Canada working outside their homes for pay, and 60 per cent of them had children under 16 years of age. When I brought up this subject earlier it was not during debate on this bill. It was on another bill which I admit was a bit off the mark, but the minister at that time was kind enough to tell me this was an important problem which would have to be debated some time. I think this is the time to do that, and today I want at least to broach the subject.
It stands to reason that since 1965 the numbers of such women have increased. The cost of living has forced more and more women into the labour market, and there are many more women employed today who have preschool children. I have two specific recommendations I would like to urge with respect to this problem in connection with the manpower training program.
These are not my ideas only. I have discussed the problems with people in a good many walks of life and people in many capacities, including the manpower training capacity. I urge that wherever women are taking manpower courses there should be established, as part of the manpower training
April 25. 1967

centre, a child care centre. This should be done in order to make it possible for women with pre-school children to attend training classes free in the knowledge that their homes and children will not be neglected.
I use the name child care centre. It could be called a creche, a nursery school or a day care centre, but I believe the name child care centre combines all the elements of these others and is a more flexible way of putting the best of these three ideas together. I suggest that this be done in order to protect the children involved.
In this connection I am going to give a few examples from this capital city in which we live because it is typical of Canadian cities. Ottawa is by no means our largest city, nor is it the smallest. Of course it is the capital. Quite recently its welfare council produced an excellent report on day care needs.
A mother in Ottawa who is going to take manpower training, if she wants to place a child under ordinary care, will have to pay $40 to $60 a month to have the child looked after during the daytime, or $10 to $15 a week. It will cost her $100 a month to have two children looked after. If she wants a housekeeper it will cost her $125 to $150 a month for a housekeeper to look after two or more children. Obviously therefore, with the proposed manpower training allowance of $35 to $90 a week she is not going to be able to afford proper care for her children. In such a case what happens to the children?
I wish to quote from a report in the Ottawa Journal of April 23, 1966, just a year ago, to tell the story:
Recently in an address delivered to the Ottawa Day Nursery annual meeting, J. A. Messner ot the Children's Aid Society, pointed out that Ottawa's six day nurseries care for no more than 260 children. As many as 160 children are being left more or less unattended while parents work. Another 1,500 children are probably being left in less than ideal substitute care.
According to Mr. Messner's reckoning, 13 per cent of children are being cared for by their mothers while at work; only 2 per cent are placed in day care centres or after school centres; while the care of the remaining 85 per cent remains unknown.
I am suggesting that one of our manpower training needs is to see to it that the children of mothers who are taking manpower training are looked after adequately in child care centres attached to the manpower training centres. This is necessary for the well-being of the children, and it is necessary to have the mothers safeguarded as students, because no mother worthy of her name as a mother can
Occupational Training
settle down to do manpower training, or work of any kind, if she does not know where her children are and how they are being protected.
As a second measure, I would urge the establishment of manpower training courses for nursery school helpers. In this connection I do not want to raise any problems about supervisors with the Nursery School Association. The supervisors In nursery schools and child care centres have to be properly trained people, preferably with a university degree. Such courses are provided in Carleton University and in other universities in various parts of the country. I do not quarrel with that. It is something which is essential for nursery school supervisors, but I do not believe it is essential for nursery school helpers.
Nursery school helpers should be comprised of two kinds of people. I believe that women with children, or children who have grown up, older women, who are badly short of income and who need a job, should take courses in being nursery school helpers, and then take jobs as nursery school helpers. Women who have married and who have raised their own families successfully would be very suitable to become nursery school helpers, and such jobs would provide them with an income. They would make up one group.
Then there are the girls who have found that high school does not hold their interest and who drop out after grade 10. I know some people might argue that they would not make good nursery school helpers. But a couple of years ago the United States had a national conference on day care centres, and a number of people occupied in the field of nursery care believed courses in child care should be offered to high school drop-outs, and graduates, in order to increase the supply of child care workers. If, with all the experience that the United States has in this field, it can urge such a step, I think we should experiment with it here in Canada.
There is another excellent reason for urging such a step. We in Canada talk about the need for safeguarding the home. We say the home is being subjected to all kinds of pressures, not the least of which are insufficiently trained young folk who get married without having experience of proper home care. I can think of no better help for young mothers and young families than for the mothers before marriage to become trained as nursery school

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
assistants under our manpower training program, and to have practical experience in a nursery school.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
I believe this would be an excellent idea. I think it would be met with favour by women in all parts of this country. I see no reason why it could not be done. After all, these are the people who will be seeking employment and who will be the future mothers and heads of the many families which are supported by one parent. I should like to suggest that in this country we are a long way from achieving the progress which has been achieved in a number of other countries in this regard. I could mention what is being done in Australia, Switzerland, Sweden, Great Britain and in other countries. They have explored these courses in day care training. I believe this is something which could be done under our manpower training. There is a great shortage in this field.
I should like to return to the Ottawa Welfare Council report. This report refers to three sources of information-the International Labour Office, Public Health Papers, and the World Health Organization. The report quotes as follows:
Today, for a variety of reasons, the need for child care facilities and services is greater throughout the world than it has ever been in the past. It is increasingly appreciated that such facilities and services are essential not only from the standpoint of child welfare and development but also from that of economic and social development in general.
Then further on we find the following in regard to Ottawa:
A survey made in 1965 through 17 primary schools' health services (Public and Separate Schools) revealed 1,098 children characterized as having day care needs, and only one child having had the benefit of a day nursery. There were 288 of pre-school age. On both counts the centre of town had the largest concentration of both school age and pre-school age.
It is all very well to ask why we should not put these mothers back into the homes so that they would be able to look after their children. These mothers are away from the homes in order to earn the money which is absolutely necessary for their livelihood. In some cases they are earning the money which is necessary to supplement the family income in the face of rising prices and living costs. It is not a question of whether these mothers shall be placed back in the home or left out. The choice is whether when they are out of their homes the homes will be neglected or whether we will provide the kind of child

care training which is necessary if their children are to be provided for. Here is another quotation:
Statistics for Ottawa produced in 1961 by D.B.S. showed 7,016 working mothers from husband-wife families had 13,325 children 15 and under at home. The D.B.S. estimates that half of these mothers had pre-school age children. Therefore at least 3,500 mothers in Ottawa, working outside their homes, have pre-school children.
If anyone should suggest that a case cannot be made for such woman power training, I should like to say that I do not know where training is more necessary. This training should be an essential part of our manpower training courses at this time. I could go on. Here is another quotation:
In the metropolitan area in 1961 there were 1,477 children aged 0-5 in one-parent families headed by women. Of these 1,283 children were from the city of Ottawa. There were also 3,889 children between 6 and 14, of whom 2,846 were in Ottawa. It is assumed that whether or not these mothers were working many of them might have needed day care services.
Social agencies doing family counselling recognize the value of day care as a strengthening measure for family life. The facilities are not available no matter how acute the need. As a result families are broken and children suffer unnecessarily.
I should like to appeal to the minister. I believe he has a heart; perhaps it is because, since he has not been on the government bench too long, he has not yet lost it. In any event we in this party believe he has shown in many ways that he has a heart. He has shown this by his views about people being able to enter this country without discrimination and by his views concerning training. It is true that he has fallen down on some things; but who does not fall down occasionally?
I believe a terrific need exists. Half the people of this country are women. Their needs are tremendous because a large percentage of them ultimately have the double burden of having to worry about the family income as well as the well-being of their children. Women should not have to be torn apart through attempting to do two jobs at the same time when they know they are not doing justice to either. No woman can perform both functions adequately without help.
For these reasons and because there is time to bring about changes in respect of the flexibility of the courses since the program is still not law, I would urge the minister to visit my province so that he may learn how the people feel. If he is afraid of the premier, then he could find some place in the province where
April 25, 1967

he would have an opportunity to speak to the people. He would find a warm reception to the idea of training courses being made available for nursery school personnel, for the older women, and for those young girls who are fresh out of school and who need training in a very real and effective way so that they will be able to perform one of the most important occupations of their lives.
