subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.

speechtext: Ths house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien (for Mr. Marchand) for the second reading of Bill No. C-278 respecting the occupational training of adults.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as was said this afternoon, this is indeed one of the more important issues that we have faced in this session. One might even be inclined to say that this might be the most important issue in terms of its long range effects for the over-all good of the country. It is for that reason that it should not be passed over lightly, and I think it is somewhat tragic that it should have been dealt with in such a cavalier fashion to date. We are in fact dealing with a matter of great consequence to many millions of our citizens, a matter which affects their very livelihood, and affects their

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
training and education. Yet, somehow or other, for no explainable reason, this whole matter has been handled in a very confused and misleading way by the government which has almost refused to discuss overtly this important legislation with the very people with whom it hopes to co-operate.
I for one find it difficult to understand why it is that we should be discussing legislation in this chamber under which regulations have already been in force for some 25 days. If this is a foretaste of things to come, then parliament has again been put in the back seat in terms of its involvement and participation in the decision making which affects this country. Not only does it extend to this chamber but it extends to all the ten provinces as well. I remember hearing my own director of vocational training say to me, when he attended a most recent conference on these regulations, with regard to the attitude of the federal agencies, "We were handed the regulations and told these are what will apply; there is very little point in discussing them in terms of any changes that might be made."
We are faced in fact with a strange problem in that, unlike most legislation, the regulations are in force before we have even passed the bill. This gives rise to questions as to what will happen in this place if an amendment is put and accepted; or does the government simply conclude that no amendments shall be accepted, regardless of their validity?
Last night the parliamentary secretary who was acting for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) told us that the explanation for doing this was that the details of such regulations are in fact spelled out in the estimates. I conclude therefore that the details under vote 5 must read as follows:
Administration, operation and maintenance, including the administration of the manpower mobility regulations and payments in respect of persons who are being afforded occupational training under the adult occupational training program in accordance with regulations approved by the governor in council.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Those few skimpy, paltry words are inadequate enough to deal with these regulations, but I think it is even more reprehensible when we remember that the only way in which these estimates have been handled to date for 1967-68 is through one month's interim supply, which allowed no time, as I recall it, for attention to be paid to the important questions of adult manpower training.
[Mr. MacDonald (Prince) .J
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) began his remarks this afternoon by talking about co-operative federalism. He said perhaps we had passed out of that era. There have been comments in the press recently to the effect that we have a new wave in this cabinet. Perhaps the era of co-operative federalism is dead, because we have witnessed twice today, I think, a new kind of federalism which can only be described, for want of a better definition, as the Trudeau-Marchand federalism in which we let the experts make all the basic decisions and the people's representatives in parliament act as a great, big 265- person rubber stamp. If that is the kind of federalism we have introduced into this house, I think we should open up that matter for very serious debate both in the house and in public circles. I for one wholeheartedly disagree with that principle and feel it is just one more opportunity for the people's wishes to pass out of their hands into the purview of experts who are installed on some lofty perches unavailable to the people, thus further alienating them in terms of participation in their own democracy.
What are the aspects of this new kind of Trudeau-Marchand federalism? There are at least four or five I can think of. First of all, it is that when you decide to do something, you make sure that you do not consult overtly with the people who will be involved, for fear the conclusions that have already been drawn up with your experts will in some way be immeasurably changed. Second, in order not to disturb things even further, you make sure that the matter is introduced quickly into parliament, by passing any possibility of parliamentary discussion in committee where a thorough examination might be given to these highly important matters. Here we have, for instance, a bill that has not been on the order paper very long. Perhaps I should not use the word "long", since I came into this house at the same time as the minister, but it is somewhat naive to introduce a resolution on March 3 with the expectation that you will have regulations in force for the new act on April 1.
This does not square with parliamentary practice and tradition as we have known it in the past. Indeed, one can think of bill after bill passed in this house where literally months, and sometimes even years have gone by before regulations have been brought into effect, with no apologies, mind you, from any government. All of a sudden within a matter of days we find our government quite willing
April 25, 1967

to bring in regulations, put them into effect and then attempt to match up whatever legislation they might like to push through the house.
Further, as I said, this new kind of federalism seems to be of a kind that says you must do things quickly. We must not let people think about them too long either in this house or in public circles. Fourth, it would seem that at the heart of some aspects of this new Trudeau-Marchand federalism there is even the suggestion that we might be making some new definitions with respect to the constitution. May I quote one comment from the minister's remarks on March 3 when he stated in this house:
The education of youth is a provincial, not a federal responsibility.
This is almost one of those accepted things that does not bear repeating in our country today unless there is some subtle meaning to it, unless we are to draw from that comment some kind of reference or meaning which, in the context of what we are asked to look at in this bill, seems to suggest that education or training for adults will in fact be the responsibility of the federal government. I have not seen these matters dealt with at any federal-provincial conference. I do not recall discussing these matters in the house. I do not even recall lengthy speeches being made on the subject by those who might be enthusiastic about this proposition.
Finally, this new kind of federalism has in it marks of a new kind of government, as implied by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) this afternoon, where the experts, whoever they may be, are settling all our constitutional problems and at the appropriate moment they may deliver these good things as manna falling from heaven; so we have almost managed to produce legislation which does not need to be passed by this house because it is already working out nicely, thank you, with regulations that have been in effect for some 25 days. One might even question why the minister should have bothered bringing this matter before the house, if his regulations are working out so effectively. If that is the case, surely there is no need to waste the time of parliament to rubber stamp the machinery of his department.
There is a great deal more to this bill and this whole matter than simply a consideration of the way in which parliament seems very effectively to have been bypassed. There is the substance of the issue that is raised. The minister, and others perhaps speaking for
Occupational Training
him, have been making great point lately in clearly delineating a difference between training and education. I suppose the thought here is that education applies to a broad subject of cultural values, of one's own awareness of his total well-being and development, whereas training has specific application to a person's employment and his work.
There may come a day, and it perhaps is coming quite rapidly, when we can draw that nice, happy, simple line between these two areas. Perhaps the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) when he discusses the guaranteed minimum income and its implications will say yea to that sentiment. But the fact of the matter is that today, in 1967, and I think for a number of years to come, the distinction the minister and others make between education and training is not a valid one, because basically whether a person is referring to his own education or his own training, it is by and large directed toward his future, or ongoing employment, and it is employment that concerns us this evening. I think it has been a phony division, to draw a line between training and education, because I do not think it squares with the reality of the situation as it exists today. The minister in his remarks of March 3 said at another point:
From here on, vocational training ranks with work; it is no longer assooiated with unemployment or welfare.
I think in those few remarks he was perhaps laying the groundwork which has proved by and large to be unwise. Surely one of the reasons we are considering this bill this evening, one of the reasons the minister has been so anxious to get his regulations into effect, is that we are indeed concerned with the question of unemployment and the problems it has raised, not only the basic fact of unemployment itself but what has been happening to people year after year when they have become almost accustomed to living for a part of the year on unemployment insurance, and the kind of negative effect that has been having on people and their creativity.
If we cannot somehow correlate the question of unemployment and unemployment insurance with the need for training and skilled development we will have an act that surely in many areas will simply not meet the needs of people who should be benefitting under this legislation. Further, the minister said in the same speech in the house on March 3:
The resolution proposes to extend training services and training allowances to all persons with adult responsibilities who can benefit from training.

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
There, it seems to me, he has made a very-clear-cut statement, that the legislation he is introducing is going to benefit all persons with adult responsibilities who can benefit from training. He goes even further, if the point has not been made clear by then, because he says:
The program will respond directly to the person's need for training-
I emphasize this last part:
-not to his statistical classification.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Now, I think that those are words with which I can wholeheartedly concur. The tragedy of the minister's own words in this regard is that they have been denied in this legislation and in the regulations that he has introduced. I am told, for instance, that in the program we have been operating over the last year, of the many hundreds of people who have been benefited from the initial program of manpower training, as many as two thirds will be ineligible for any kind of major benefit under the program the minister has introduced. This results from the regulations that define an adult. This definition, in itself, is interesting, Mr. Speaker. I am not sure whether this is the first time we have started to define an adult as other than a person who has reached 21 years of age. We now have a new definition of an adult as one who has been out of school for a year. Does this mean that a 12 year old child who has dropped out of school for a year is an adult? Does this mean that a person who is 25 or 26 years of age and is still pursuing training has not yet become an adult? Surely there are a number of anomalies in the definition of an adult as set out in this legislation.
Certainly I find in both the bill and the regulations an inflexibility that is difficult to understand and is almost intolerable. Why should we be anxious and willing to introduce a program which the minister knows, because of the correspondence he has received, will mean that province after province will have to disfranchise many of the people who would benefit from it? Ontario talks about 7,000 students who will immediately be cast aside because of the specifics that the federal government feels should be honoured by provinces like Ontario. In Prince Edward Island, where perhaps only 500 students are directly involved in this program, at least 300 will be set aside because of the inflexibility of these regulations.
Even stranger is the effect this program may have on another aspect of the minister's

own department. We are told, for instance, that immigrants coming into the country will be regarded the same as Canadian citizens, for inclusion in this program, if they have been on the labour market for three years, I believe, without dependants, or one year with dependants. They will then be automatically acceptable to this program for job retraining and skill development.
I should like to ask the minister this question. In many European countries, as he well knows, young boys-and they are boys-of 14 go on the labour market because their formal education ends at an earlier period. It is more than conceivable that many young men of 17 or 18 will come to this country as immigrants and will be immediately available for this kind of training, while many young people in this country who have become drop-outs, who have not been able to cope with academic problems, who are of the same age and apparently have the same qualifications, will have to wait for as much as three years before they can acquire the same benefits that are being made available to those who come to reside in this country. Here is one case where we have a reversal of the pattern. We are quite willing to be fairer to those who come to Canada than to those who are native citizens.
Further, I for one am quite depressed by the fact the minister has announced that as of April 1, I believe, the encouragement and activities that have gone on in his department to further training at the secondary school level will be abandoned, by reason of the rather paradoxical suggestion at this late date that it is not, after all, his constitutional responsibility. One could well raise the question of why the department entered into it in the first place, if it has now concluded it is no longer its constitutional responsibility. I wonder when we shall have an opportunity, in fact, to discuss the constitutional responsibility exercised by the department of manpower.
There is another strange paradox in this bill and in these regulations, because we are told that further money will be made available for capital grants. I believe this will mean a further, final allotment of some $4.5 million to Prince Edward Island. This amount is more than twice the required amount to construct further schools in Prince Edward Island, which in many cases will not be needed in view of the facilities that have already been established there. The failing is, I think, that we will make money available for further capital resources, whether or not they will be needed, and yet we are withdrawing from
April 25, 1967

some areas where it is vitally needed the assistance for operating expenses to carry on this important program.
Certainly, to the province of Prince Edward Island, which has a very slim tax base, this is a great set-back for its future vocational training program, to realize that there are many millions of dollars set aside for capital resources which will not be constructed, when the kind of assistance that is needed is operating grants. These operating grants cannot be made available because of the inflexibility that has been introduced into this program. I believe that in view of the necessity for academic training, we have been talking about giving certain upgrading courses to those who wish to improve their arithmetic and English in grade 9 and 10. Is the minister actually being realistic when he thinks that those who enter the labour market in the next five or ten years, even with some kind of skilled training and with partial grade 9 or 10, are going to find ready employment on the labour market? I believe he is not. I believe that shortly we will be faced with passing further legislation to deal with this short-sighted situation.
In addition, I believe we have tackled only one area of the necessity for manpower training. Surely it is an important thing, as we have been told in this house and will be told again, to provide the kind of opportunities we will provide for those who are now in the labour market, in terms of removing themselves from the labour market for a year, or perhaps two. However, I am concerned to see a program developed that will assist those who may not have to leave completely their specific job, but who could make use of night training or week end courses which would augment their present information and expertise. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we should be introducing that kind of flexibility in our program if it is going to meet the varied needs of the different skills and occupations across this country.
Further, we are told that the federal government is going to be able, under this new bill, to lend money to the provincial governments which they may use to erect various structures. Then, over a period of 30 years, the money will be repaid through yearly grants. This is a new, strange and complex way of financing, and it introduces some questions which have perhaps never been raised before. I would think the 30 year plan of rental and loan is based on the assumption
Occupational Training
that we will be operating, by and large, under this kind of legislation for the next 30 years.
Surely the minister knows that he is involved in one of the most dynamically changing aspects of society, man and his work. We can barely predict what kind of employment opportunities, what kind of skills will be needed five years from now; yet we are going to commit the provinces to a 30 year ownership of facilities. What kind of planning is that? Some governments, I do not know whether it will be provincial or federal, will be stuck with millions of dollars worth of hardware that will be out of date and obsolescent.
Earlier the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie), in commenting on the need for more co-ordination, mentioned the fact we should very carefully examine how this program will relate to such a program as ARDA. I believe that is very wise advice indeed. I am struck again and again with the way in which government departments seem to operate, in many instances, in isolated ghettos. They have no real idea of the sort of thing that may be happening in other departments or how they could effectively harmonize with one another.
An even more important aspect of the ARDA program that should be considered is found in the Rural Economic Development program, or FRED as it is euphemistically called and which will, in fact, be involved in a major transformation of areas of great economic necessity. However, there has been no recognition that I have been able to discover of that fact in the bill or the regulations before us.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I think it is important when we deal with this legislation that we be given some assurance that in making provision for many aspects of this manpower training program, provision will be made also for giving assistance to the provinces in connection with the administration of this program. In larger provinces this may not be any great problem, for I know their vocational training divisions and departments have many officers, a great many provincial experts and the opportunity effectively to administer this kind of program.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Yet it is true, Mr. Speaker, that although you establish a program which may work effectively in a large province like Ontario, Quebec or British Columbia, when you come to a relatively poorer province like Prince Edward Island the administrative cost can be

April 25, 1967
Occupational Training
an overwhelming burden and can well prevent a great deal of the program from becoming operative. Therefore I hope that the minister during the course of this debate will assure us that some recognition will be given to the problem of administrative cost in small and economically deprived provinces like Prince Edward Island.
In summary, let me simply say that I think this legislation is too important to be slipped through quickly, simply following the regulations which have already come into effect. I think it is important that we recognize that this is a matter of great national consequence. If the opportunity does not present itself tonight or within the next day or so to discuss the question of education, training and the responsibilities of federal and provincial government, then we must be given that opportunity soon. It is not enough to slip through some regulations and to bring in a bill without giving any consideration to the kind of precedents that we are setting or policies that we are following. We should not establish a whole new trend in federal-provincial relations without considering where we are going and when we hope to arrive.
It is also a little disturbing to realize that despite what I think the government would admit is its considerable inexperience in the field of education the government at Ottawa has been willing in this instance to make unilateral decisions with very little opportunity for consultation or creative discussion with the various provincial representatives.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, from meeting with other members the secret of this program, it seems to me, is found in its flexibility; and even the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has talked about this recently. If we try to lay down hard and fast guide lines in Ottawa to accommodate ten provinces which are vastly different in their capabilities, we will introduce and pass a law here which will be a very sad thing indeed for many of the provinces. The minister's colleague in this house, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau), remarked shortly after his appointment that he had not been in the cabinet long enough to change his mind. I trust that the minister of manpower has been in the cabinet long enough to change his mind. I do not think it is a sign of weakness not to be able to change one's mind. I think it shows right thinking. I think it shows a willingness to grapple with the issues as they present themselves and to pass the best legislation possible.
[Mr. MacDonald (Prince).}

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliameniary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the minister, who is a relatively new member of this house, for the impact he has had on the House of Commons in the short time he has been here, for the impact he has had on a new department and, more particularly, for the influence he has had on federal-provincial relations in this country. I think that that influence has been all to the good. He is now the minister responsible for manpower, one might even say the minister responsible for opportunities, certainly those opportunities that are open to adults in this country.
If we have anything in Canada, we have resources. We also have a lot of machines. We are told by the Economic Council of Canada that we have more machines per capita, certainly per employee, than any other country in the world, including the United States. We seem to have markets for many of our products but we are short of manpower. We have only 20 million people on a large half continent, and it is the way that we husband these human resources which will determine our economic progress in the months and years ahead.
Ours is a new country, Mr. Speaker. It is a country of great opportunity in terms of resources, in terms of new industries, in terms of occupations. In order to take full advantage of these new resources, industries and occupations our labour force has to be mobile. To be mobile it has to be educated. It has to develop new skills and through these new skills earn the greater returns that come to labour from these new endeavours. Canada must have policies which encourage education, and encourage mobility; and these are the type of policies which the present minister of manpower has been introducing.
Compartmentalization, in other words, is not for us. It cannot be the policy followed in a relatively young country like Canada. Compartmentalization in many areas means that we are not taking full advantage of those opportunities that are open to us. Compartmentalization can take many forms. It can be compartmentalization in respect to occupation; it can be compartmentalization in respect to the industry in which one is working; and in this country particularly it can be compartmentalization in the sense of being rooted to one locality or region. It means not being mobile enough to move to other areas where productivity is higher, where wages
April 25, 1967

are better and where the profitability of industry is on the increase.
Programs such as those incorporated by this bill lead toward this greater flexibility, this opportunity through education for our adult population. This program must be seen, of course, in conjunction with the manpower mobility program; but the two in harness provide us with an opportunity to make the best of our scarcest resource, which is manpower. We have the markets, we have the machines and often we have the money, but rarely do we have the manpower. Certainly we are short of skilled manpower.
I made reference at the outset of my remarks to federal-provincial relations. This area of education is always touchy because the British North America Act provides that education is a matter exclusively for the provinces. But education, I contend, as defined in the year 1867, is education of the very young, not of the adult, the mature Canadian, the person who, having come of age, should decide where he works, what his vocation is, and in what part of the country he resides. This is one of the reasons I welcome a rough division or breakdown in responsibilities in respect to education: education of the very young remaining the responsibility of the provinces; education, the training and opening up of opportunities for adults being a matter for the nation.
There are various definitions of the word "nation". They are areas in the world in which there is free trade in commodities- goods and services. They are areas through which there is free movement of capital. They are also areas through which the people of the countries concerned can move without serious impediment. We have seen a great improvement in manpower mobility in this country in recent years. The decline in unemployment in itself has helped people to move. The Canada Pension Plan and other measures to integrate welfare legislation provincially across the country have helped to make it easier for people to uproot themselves from one occupation, from one industry, and from one area often with a relatively low wage rate, to others which are more productive, whose industries pay more and where opportunities for one to make full use of his talents are greater, and more satisfying.
We have had through the National Employment Service and we now have through the manpower service centres the provision of
Occupational Training
information for people who cannot be expected by themselves to know where the best job opportunities are located across the country. The role of the manpower centres in explaining to the public and certainly to the labour force where these new opportunities lie is a crucial one.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
It is a very difficult role to play, and the Economic Council of Canada itself is providing some guidance in this respect. The provincial economic councils can supplement this information, but the manpower centres will have to be very ingenuous and work closely with industry if they are to determine precisely what skills are required five or ten years in the future and where these sources of employment are, these opportunities to upgrade one's skill, these opportunities to satisfy the drives and ambitions of our people to better themselves, their families and their communities.
We have problems in this country, problems of adjustment between growth industries and industries which have either begun to level off or to decline. We must enable our manpower to shift itself as between these dying industries and the more dynamic industries which have growth opportunities. If these industries, the growth industries and the dying industries, were to be found side by side this would be easier; but in Canada, a country of vast distances, we have the problem of our five major geographic regions; and within those regions we have areas which have been designated as areas of slow growth, with other areas having greater opportunities.
The Economic Council has done a reasonable job in describing what has been happening in Canada, and the picture is not encouraging. Roughly, it is this: For the last 40 years, the years for which the Economic Council can find statistics, the relative income levels as between one part of the country and another have remained unchanged. The Atlantic region, in per capita income terms, has been 25 per cent below the national average since the early 1920's, so far as the Economic Council can determine Ontario and British Columbia, in per capita income terms, have run 25 per cent above the national average. In other words, we have areas which pay more and have been paying more than some other areas, and we have areas which have greater employment opportunities and less unemployment than other areas.

April 25. 1967
Occupational Training
In pure economics one would expect a shift of people from the low income areas to the high income areas; and indeed that is what has slowly been happening in this country. However, despite the selective and specific policies introduced by successive governments, the margin between the Atlantic region and Ontario, or between Quebec and British Columbia has not changed very much. The situation has been described by the Economic Council in a series of charts which show parallel lines running up across the page. These parallel lines stand in strong contrast to those shown for the United States, where the differences of income between regions have been narrowing. We need to know more about why in the United States the income levels as between the deep south and the industrial north have been converging, and why the differences between the Atlantic seaboard and the United States west coast have been disappearing. Why have these regional differences been disappearing in the United States, and why have they been so persistent in Canada?
I might question whether some of our policies have been effective or well advised. Today we are in much better shape than we were in four or five years ago. We had to introduce special policies four or five years ago to employ people; to employ people, first, was all important. Now it is becoming increasingly important to make that employment more productive and efficient.
People should be moving out of the declining industries, out of the relatively static industries, into the growth industries of this country. That is the sort of function the national manpower centres must perform. They can perform this function, as I say, by advising people who want to better themselves, who want to know where new skills are required, what those skills are and where the growing opportunities are for those skills and occupations. They want to know the industries and the areas of the country where those skills are required. Knowing that, they can become more productive. It is that sort of opportunity that Bill No. C-278 describes-the opportunity whereby people can take time off from their jobs, at a moderate wage rate so to speak, and be retrained with an eye on a job that improves their prospects in the years ahead.
It is interesting to note that the differences in income across Canada which are so marked roughly parallel the differences in the education of the people. British Columbia has the highest educational standard in Canada in

terms of number of years at school, and it pays the highest wage rates. Ontario is close to British Columbia. As I said before, the average per capita incomes in British Columbia and Ontario are almost the same. Quebec's average is a bit below the national average, being 25 per cent below Ontario and British Columbia. It is below Alberta and below Saskatchewan. The Atlantic provinces are lower again.
I suggest that the inevitable result of programs of this kind is to enable people to move to those industries and those areas with the highest rate of growth. People will also move toward the bigger communities, the bigger cities and towns; they will tend to move west as they have done in the United States. The centre of gravity of the population has been moving westward year after year. That movement is inevitable because greater opportunities lie in the west at the present time.
We need manpower centres; we need assistance for the retraining of adults to bring about this great improvement in productivity and to make our people more mobile. There is great talk, especially in Europe and on other continents, of free trade areas and common markets. The mobility of people on the European continent today is much greater than it was five or ten years ago, and ten years from now that mobility will be greater again. People will be freer to move in those new viable, vigorous expanding economies. You will also find the more productive industries in those great free trade areas.
Canada, by degrees I am sure, will enter into freer trading arrangements with other countries. It may also enter into special arrangements, industrial arrangements from time to time, with the United States.
What this increased competition means is change; and what change means is that production lines will be retooled, new plants will be built, some industries will go to the wall and others will take their place. This means that people must be told where the growth industries are, what the growth opportunities for their occupations are, and what they should be readying themselves for in the future. They must be told of the jobs which are most rewarding in so far as their own talents are concerned.
I do not think we can afford compartmen-talization in this country either in terms of regional economics or provincial economics. We must not have a compartmentalization of industries, with some industries being favoured unduly over the taxpayers' expense;
April 25, 1967

nor must we have favouritism of other kinds which will unduly segment our country and reduce the opportunities to Canadians which would otherwise be theirs.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I will say this to the minister: The hon. gentleman has, through this bill, given us legislation which will make this country more viable and which will make it a better place for Canadians to live in. He has broadly staked out an area, one which 1 call training, which is truly federal. It will help to increase mobility within the totality of Canada. It will afford an opportunity for self-improvement to all Canadians, regardless of where they live or what work they are doing today. The bill itself is well drawn up and I find no fault with the provision by which young people must have left school for at least three years before they can take advantage of this program. I do not find fault with the provision that those who are married and have dependants should receive special preference in this regard.
There is one clause which worries me a little; it is on the fines of a clause which creeps into a good deal of our legislation, and it has to do with rates of pay for those who are being retrained. In effect these rates are tied to the national average for all Canada as published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
Under this system people in the higher income areas will not find the level of pay as attractive as those in the lower income areas. Perhaps this will serve as a bonus or incentive to those in the lower wage areas to look for new jobs, to upgrade their skills and join the trend of the future. Perhaps we shall have to five with a national norm, but with this exception I am all in favour of the legislation before us. It is a useful bill tending to bind this country more closely together and make it more productive. By staking out clearly an area of federal responsibility and knitting it in carefully with provincial responsibilities and commitments in the field of education the Minister of Manpower and Immigration has gone a long way toward making this country a better country in which to live.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words about Bill C-278 because I consider that the training of our labour force is an extremely important matter, and its solution the key to our economic situation and to the well-being of our labour force.
Occupational Training
I do not intend to deal minutely with the provisions of this bill because a great deal of criticism has already been expressed with regard to the arbitrary manner in which the regulations were set forth prior to the passing of the legislation before us. Then again, some of my hon. friends have drawn attention to the almost violent criticism which has been forthcoming from the provinces, whose administrators are far better versed in the educational and training aspects of these proposals than anyone in the federal government. Since my hon. friends have dealt with many of the particular aspects of this matter, and its shortcomings, I intend to deal in general terms with the subject of training as a Whole.
The opportunities for labour were excellent, I must say, in the field of education and training generally under the legislation introduced and expanded during our term of office, from 1960 onward. The present minister has accepted these policies and is carrying them on. In some areas he has made changes, and the effect of certain of these changes appears to be detrimental rather than an improvement of the work which was started and accelerated during our term of office.
It is well, on occasions, to discard one's modesty and to tell the history of certain things which have taken place. I intend to do this by discarding my modesty tonight 

something I seldom do in this house-so as to remind hon. members of what was done during our administration with respect to the training and retraining of the labour force. In 1959 and 1960, after a careful survey had been made of the economic situation which had been left with us when we took office, it was found by the economists that only 30 per of all the jobs available in Canada called for unskilled labour. This was an alarming situation because many of those in our labour force were not equipped with the skills which had become necessary as a result of technological change and automation.
Moreover, it was predicted that 30 per cent of the unskilled jobs available would diminish year after year as progress was made in the field of technological change. Something had to be done, and in consultation with the provinces where jurisdiction over education properly lies we took this matter up. We were told that the provinces were prepared to undertake a program of retraining, provided they could acquire facilities which they did not then possess.
In order to make those facilities available, a bill was introduced in this house in

a great mistake, Mr. Speaker. The program under the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act should have been carried on and accelerated over the years because the important thing is that the facilities must be provided before training can be provided.
When we were in government we prepared a bill, separate from the technical assistance bill, to provide on-the-job training for those displaced by technological change and automation in industry. Unfortunately that bill was still on the order paper when we were turned out of office in 1963, and now the present government is sneaking in similar provisions under clause 6 of this bill. This is a move forward, but I believe the minister should call a conference of labour and management to get their ideas as to what type of regulations should be drafted. The co-operation of labour and management is needed, as well as co-operation between the provinces and the federal government.
This should not be a hard and fast piece of legislation; it should be flexible. However, the regulations that have been put into effect prior to the passing of the bill have provoked an outcry from provincial governments. In my opinion the provinces, with their experience, should know whether this bill will work or not, and since there has been an outcry from some of them I believe their representations should be heard, because education and training rightly fall under their jurisdiction. Why was no conference called prior to the issuing and the putting into effect of the regulations?
I read a newspaper report recently which said:
Ontario education minister William Davis wrote Mr. Marchand expressing concern over the apparently arbitrary manner in which Ottawa was determined to lay down its new act. Mr. Davis warned that if chaos were to be avoided, a high-level meeting should be convened without delay.
That report appeared in the Globe and Mail of Saturday, April 22. In the Ontario legislature last Thursday Mr. Davis again requested a meeting with the federal minister, and later said he was sure a solution could be found to the crisis. However, I have yet to read that the federal minister has paid any heed to this warning or that he is prepared to call such a meeting to be attended by the provincial ministers of education.
Why has there been no conference? Why has this bill been put forward in such an arbitrary way, without the knowledge of the provinces and without their participation in
Occupational Training
any talks prior to the issuance of the regulations? Where is all this co-operative federalism that the government has been talking about for so long? I know the minister believed in co-operative federalism, but something has happened and now we see this bill being pushed through with no evidence of co-operative federalism. Why has the minister taken this autocratic attitude? Why is he putting it to the provinces on the basis of "take it or leave it"?
In the light of this, and in view of the apprehension that has been expressed since the regulations were issued, the minister should seriously consider withholding this bill. After all, he now has his regulations, and the bill is given to us 25 days after the regulations were issued. Is it not time to call a conference of educational ministers and try to smooth out some of their apprehensions? It might even be possible to amend some of the regulations, showing co-operative federalism at work and satisfying everyone who has to work under the regulations.
In addition to the provincial ministers of education the Indian population is irked by this bill. According to a report in the Montreal Star of today's date:
The Indian-Eskimo Association of Canada is worried that Canada's new manpower training law will deprive thousands of unemployed and underemployed Indians of job training.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The report goes on to say:
Mr. O'Connell said that more than one-half of the Indians are unemployed and many never entered the labour force. A recent survey showed that 61 per cent of a large sample group of breadwinners work less than six months a year.
He said large numbers of Indian children drop out of school before the age of 16.
How are they to qualify under the regulations? This is one more reason that the government should hold up this bill, have this conference, and iron out many of the things which are brought to our attention. As members of this House of Commons I believe it is our duty to point out these things to the minister, in case they have not as yet been brought to his attention. Another question which arises in my mind is what happens to the youngster who has been out of school for one year and has not put in three years in the labour force. This youngster will be given no benefits under the plan unless the provinces are prepared to pay his subsistence. The federal government does not intend to do this. In this regard additional costs are being added

April 25. 1967
Occupational Training
to the already overburdened provinces because of the high cost of education.
Unless this type of young person receives aid in the amount of 100 per cent from the provinces he never will be able to obtain the training which will be necessary in order to find employment or place himself in the labour force. He will never qualify. Yesterday the parliamentary secretary quoted some extracts from the minister's speech. I find these at page 15263 of Hansard of April 24. In quoting the minister he said:
These facts were made public in October at the last federal-provincial conference. It was made clear that there was nothing to prevent any province from offering allowances to younger people without dependants, if it so wishes.
In other words, he is saying to the provinces: "Look, if these people do not qualify under our regulations, you can do what you like with them; it is your baby. Part of it is our responsibility and part of it is your responsibility." This, in effect, divides the labour force. It is the same as saying that these people will be responsible to the province for their training and that others who do qualify under the federal regulations will be a federal responsibility. This is something which has never been done before.
Under all previous training programs everybody came under the one act. Why is a distinction being made in this case? Why is it said that part of the labour force will come under provincial jurisdiction so far as training is concerned and that part of it will come under federal jurisdiction? I should like to quote the minister again:
The new program will train at least as many workers as the former program did.
If the idea is to launch something which is new and revolutionary, I would think it would be suggested that it would at least double the number who will be trained or who will wish to be trained, because we are to provide the facilities. The quotation continues:
The federal government is providing larger funds-
I suppose he means by that that they are providing a larger amount of money to pay for the subsistence of those who are taking training. Evidently it does not mean anything else, because he goes on to say:
-as the provinces provide more facilities.
In other words, they are saying they will not pay the subsistence for these people unless the provinces provide the facilities.

Then, if the provinces cannot afford to provide the facilities, it will not cost the federal government a nickel, because no one will be trained. That is what it amounts to.
In view of all these matters which I have brought to the attention of the minister, in view of those which have been brought to his attention by the former speakers, and in view of the inequities which appear in this bill I can come to one conclusion only and that is that the provinces cannot afford the cost of their participation in this retraining program, and therefore that I do not believe it will be successful.
There is, therefore, only one alternative, and that is to hold up this bill and immediately hold a conference with the ministers and others who will be directly concerned with this retraining in the provinces, to see how these regulations might be improved to the advantage of everybody concerned. Let us have practical co-operative federalism as it should be practised, and not this arbitrary attitude which we find at the present time in putting forward this training bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we reach the clause by clause examination of this bill I hope the minister will take the time which may be necessary to answer some questions which have been disturbing many of us who are participating in this debate. It seems more things have been unsaid concerning this bill than have been said by its supporters.
Perhaps it is easy to see the type of problems the minister has set out to correct. We have pointed out that the federal government should take greater initiative in the field of manpower programs. We have suggested that the shared cost arrangement leaves considerable discretion with the provinces. Those provinces which have the resources are able to participate, and those which do not have the resources are unable fully to avail themselves of the training. The fact that the federal government is prepared to play its full part in this particular regard is a very hopeful sign. However when, after accepting its full share, it acts in a way which antagonizes the best friends of this program, then we must seriously question the methods it has used.
When a vast group of persons who need training desperately-some people have calculated that the number is at least 200,000 young people of this country-is eliminated because of the attempt to cover the whole cost of the program, then I believe we need some answers to explain this type of attitude.
April 25, 1967

In the past we have pointed out that the allowances were inadequate. An attempt has been made now to correct these so that they are more realistic and will enable people to carry on with their training. However, while the minister is handing out better allowances with the one hand to some groups, he is taking everything away from another group. Where is the sense in this type of approach?
Surely, while we welcome the increased allowances, we must deplore the fact that the minister has practically eliminated an entire group of people from this program. This program has been enlarged to include those who are employed as well as those who are unemployed. Again I believe this is a forward step, a good step, which will lead to an all encompassing manpower program for the future. But the provisions which I criticized before in respect of those who are absent from school, those who have been employed for three years and those who have no dependants, is a retrograde step and certainly is not one which will help our manpower policy at all.
This particular group is the most sensitive one in our society; it is the group which needs the most encouragement; it is the group which, in social terms, will cost us untold amounts and cause us untold heartache unless we do something to provide those in the group with training and opportunities.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
There does not seem to be any understanding of this kind of problem. When we try to understand the thinking of the minister in this regard we find ourselves unable to do so. Has he done this because he wanted to establish clearly what is under federal and what is under provincial jurisdiction? Did he try to draw a clean line by saying, "If you are in the work force for three years, then you are the federal government's responsibility; otherwise you are the provincial government's responsibility and the province will have to look after you"? Is there a big power play going on between the federal and provincial governments? Do we have two bulls butting at each other to see who gets hurt first? I hope the people who need retraining are not in the middle or else they will get crushed. I hope the minister will examine this bill and make the kind of changes that I think are necessary in it. I wonder sometimes whether the minister was frightened by his own liberalism when he said, "We are going to increase the allowances, and this will cost some money. Let us get rid of a whole bunch
Occupational Training
of people, let us chuck them right out of the program so it will not cost us that much money; then we will only have to pay a relatively small amount." I hope this was not his thinking.
I hope the time has come when the importance of manpower is recognized to the extent that the government will be prepared to allocate resources to this purpose, because we can all agree that any money spent in this area will be amply repaid to the nation in terms of increased productivity which will be created in that regard. It is particularly disturbing when we read in the papers about the concern of the educators who have participated in this program from the very beginning, people who have been dedicated to doing this kind of work. I should like to read from the Kitchener-Waterloo Record of April 20 in which an article appeared concerning an interview with Mr. Charles Rushton who is the head of the adult education centre in Waterloo. He is quoted as having said the following:
Changes in the federal Adult Occupational Training Act may close the door to at least a third of the more than 800 who have been taking retraining courses at the adult education centre in Waterloo.
The changes will alter the entire philosophy of the program.
The young school drop-outs, housewives, recent widows and all those people who have not had three years in the labour force will be rejected.
I made a number of calls tonight to see whether I could get some information on how this affects people. I did not want statistics; I wanted to know how it affects these people in particular-not abstractions. For example let us take widows. There are many widows registered in these courses. They are without dependants, and many of them have not been in the work force. They cannot possibly benefit from the provisions of this act. Surely the minister must come up with some kind of answer as to how he will deal with this particular problem. There are housewives who have to go out to work because their husbands are ill or because they have family problems of one kind or another. If they have not been members of the work force, they also do not qualify under the provisions of this act. Does the minister really feel that he is promoting the manpower retraining program when he excludes people of this type, because of the rigidity of the provisions as set out in the bill?

April 25. 1967
Occupational Training
Mr. Rushton went on to say:
This seriously retards all the rehabilitative aspects of the retraining program that we have built up in the Kitchener-Waterloo area.
Counselling testing review work and personalizing the day-to-day time table of the adult are all major factors if the trainee is to be successful in his course.
I understand that as things are at present the manpower centre officers do not have the necessary experience for this kind of work. This is not to say they will not acquire it in time. I understand there are some very able and capable people in the service. However, right now they do not have the experience, and yet people who have it are not being consulted. The program has been taken out of their hands. They were told: "Look buddy, thanks for the work you have done. We do not need you any more. You will do exactly as we say, regardless of whether you are more or less qualified than you have been in the past." I do not think this is the kind of program we want to run. I do not think we are really helping by doing this sort of thing.
Farther on in the article Mr. Rushton is quoted as saying:
We are still optimistic that once the minister of manpower is made aware of the numerous fallacies in the act they will be corrected before it becomes law.
This is what we want the minister to do. We want him either to give us a reasonable explanation for his position or to make some corrections which will satisfy the objections we have raised.
I know that in the past it has been said that when people are close to the completion of their school education they will abuse this system. I can assure the house that I have studied the program five courses very carefully and have found that the number of people in that program who have behaved in this way has been infinitesimal. I think this danger is more in people's minds than it is a fact, and it is a danger of such insignificance that it would not warrant the setting up of provisions to prevent it. There are people who have gone back to program five only because they were able to obtain some assistance while they were taking the course.
I should like to read from the Kitchener-Waterloo Record of February 8, 1966. Mr. Rushton was asked how many of his pupils had difficulties-, to which he answered that more than 70 per cent of the students have serious financial and social problems, along with a lack of educatiin or skills. This means

that even if a few pupils drop out of school for a year or a lesser period in order to take the retraining course, they would not have been drawn out of school because most probably they would have dropped out of school anyway. Many of these drop-outs have to leave school for financial reasons. What is wrong with getting them back to school and offering them some financial inducements to do so?
If the minister feels that the three year requirement is necessary, then I think he should consider another program for those who have not been in the work force for three years. I think he should consider superimposing the program he is now advocating with the program we had before and thus establishing one which would be more satisfactory than the one proposed under this bill.
The editorial in the Globe and Mail issue of April 19, 1967 quotes Lieutenant Poulton of the Salvation Army as saying:
A bill before parliament threatens to wreck the rehabilitation plans of many of those youngsters.
... The bill would cut off training privileges and allowances for about 80 per cent of the teen-agers and young men enrolled in the Salvation Army's House of Concord program in Toronto.
This has been an excellent program. Its objectives were to provide a home for youths who manifest a need for more intensive supervision and closer control than is normally given in a community. It operates in conjunction with the magistrate's court.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on Bill No. C-278 but I shall be very brief so that the minister can deal with some of the problems we have raised. I can be brief because of the good points brought out by other members of my party, especially the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr). I share with him apprehension with regard to the possible curtailment of the program under the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act which was brought into effect in 1960, as the hon. member said, by the government in which he was minister of labour. The hon. member said he feared that Bill No. C-278 would sound the death knell of this technical and vocational training plan. I hope that is not correct, and I think we should take every step possible to see that it does not happen.
I agree that there is a need for adult training or retraining in this period of great technological and economic change. As the parliamentary secretary to the minister stated, retraining people whose jobs are disappearing is only part of the task. We must also train the adults who earlier were not able to get the training that is needed today. As did the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Keays) who spoke earlier, I object to the suggestion from the government side that our debate and study of the unification of the armed forces delayed consideration of other government bills. As the record shows, we proposed that the unification bill be set aside so that the house could consider more important legislation. The decision to go ahead with the unification bill was entirely the decision of the government. As has been said many times, the government sets the pace of parliament by the order in which legislation is introduced. I agree with the hon. member for Ontario that this bill should be delayed, but apparently the government will try to push it through before it is completely studied, as it has with respect to other bills.
I have said on other occasions that I regret that the government is phasing out, under a program announced recently, the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act. Under the operations of Bill C-278 we must make sure that the excellent results being obtained by the technical institutes built under the program brought in by the previous 23033-969
Occupational Training
government are continued. If I may speak in a local vein for a moment, Mr. Speaker, there is a very fine technical institute in my home city of Moose Jaw. It has all the modern training facilities, the teaching staff is highly qualified and there is room for expansion at very little cost as compared with constructing new buildings. I point this out to emphasize that to obtain the best results Bill No. C-278 should be fitted in with the facilities of the technical institutes now established.
Under this bill the federal government proposes to pay for adult training. I suggest that the government should make sure that the money to be spent on this training is used in the best way possible. In my view this can be done by the closest possible co-operation between the local Canada Manpower Centre and the technical institute. There must be teamwork between the manpower counselling service and the technical institute. As the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald) pointed out a short while ago, the government is offering loans to the provinces to erect new buildings, with the loan repayment being made over 30 years. I suggest that a much better way would be to add to the facilities of the present institutes and work them into this program.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am cutting these remarks short. I shall probably have more to say on this matter in committee when the bill is studied clause by clause. I have just one more brief observation to make. It is in regard to this statement made by the parliamentary secretary, as reported in Hansard on page 15259:
Since 1949, for instance, over half a million farmers have left Canadian agriculture.
This was a very casual and off-hand comment by the parliamentary secretary with regard to a very serious problem facing agriculture. It is a comment that cannot be accepted so casually. We have pressed the government, and shall continue to do so, for more effective solutions to farm problems than merely having farmers leave the land. I know this is not the entire responsibility of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), but I consider it is partly his problem under the manpower training program.
The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) made some comments along this line. I agree with his suggestion that adult training under this bill must be dovetailed into the ARDA program. ARDA is aimed at the best possible use of land, water and other

April 25. 1967
Occupational Training
resources. The objective of this bill should be to help farmers fit into the ARDA program. Representing an urban-rural riding, I consider that much greater effort should be made by the government to put agriculture on a more stable foundation. I shall not refer at this time to the need for some solution to the farmer's cost-price squeeze. That problem belongs to other government departments.
I suggest that the manpower training program should include a course for specialized agriculture, such as the best possible soil use, better cost accounting systems, greater production per unit and other aspects of modern agriculture. There should be training in operating irrigated land to help farmers in certain areas stay on their land. These farmers would be taught to take advantage of irrigation projects, such as the south Saskatchewan dam when it is completed. In other words, there should be a definite plan to educate young farmers to continue in agriculture rather than to allow them to leave the farm and train them for some other occupation.
I consider, Mr. Speaker, this is the part such a manpower training program could play. This is a part of manpower training which the minister has apparently overlooked. Perhaps he will comment on this aspect of the matter before second reading is given to his bill. I repeat that I consider the training of farmers in order to get them to stay on the land is more important to the economy of this country than to retrain them for other jobs after they have left the farm.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some comments to make on this Bill No. C-278, an act respecting the occupational training of adults and on the amendment introduced this afternoon by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) suggesting a tax compensation for the provinces not wishing to participate in this federal legislation on vocational training and who might prefer an independent provincial legislation, an autonomous responsibility in this area.
I hope that when the minister rises to speak he will bring some clarification to this matter.
My remarks will be brief. For most of the day, I have been listening to the speeches of the hon. members. I have noted that many of them are confused and unsure as to how far
[Mr. Pascoe.l
the central government intends to go and proceed in this vocational training of adults and how far the provinces, wishing to legislate in a similar area, will go.
We would like to know if on the whole other provinces have given up their jurisdiction or whether they have delegated their responsibilities in this field. We have learned through the newspapers in the past few months that the province of Quebec and the province of British Columbia have many reservations and have warned the federal government before the introduction of this bill against proceeding unilaterally without a definite and comprehensive agreement on all legislation in this area.
A few weeks ago, some Quebec officials came to Ottawa, among whom Mr. Claude Morin, deputy minister for federal-provincial affairs, Messrs. Arthur Tremblay and Yves Martin, deputy ministers of education and Mr. Fernand Jolicoeur, general director of permanent education. They came to Ottawa to discuss with the hon. minister or his representative, probably Mr. Kent, the occupational training of adults and related matters, and probably explain to the central government that the province of Quebec is deeply concerned with the matter and intends to guard jealously its authority and autonomy in that field.
I do not know whether there was any correspondence exchanged between the minister and the various provincial governments, but I suggest it would be most interesting if such correspondence, if any, were tabled, so that we might be in a position to find out in this house whether all the provinces agreed with the provisions of this legislation or, if they did not, to see what one or more provinces objected to and what their plans are in this field.
As pointed out several times today, it would not be desirable for both levels of government, that is federal and provincial, to operate and compete in the same field, as this could give rise to constitutional crises or conflicts which we must seek to avoid, in order to achieve better harmony in Canada between Canadians and the various governments.
Did the minister state clearly the responsibilities of the central government and those of the provincial governments when he met the provincial representatives, especially those from the province of Quebec?
April 25, 1967

I hope that, in his speech, the minister will tell us about the talks he had and the correspondence he received. That is very important because Canadians must not have the impression that, in the House of Commons, the government is trying to introduce a measure without the approval and the understanding of all the provinces and their population.
The policy trend of the various governments in the field of occupational training of adults should be quite clear in the minds of both federal and provincial administrators.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, this piece of legislation points to the urgency of defining the responsibilities of the various governments.
Members of various parties have often asked the government during our debates or the question period to establish a joint parliamentary committee on constitutional reform but, unfortunately, the answers given by the government have been unsatisfactory to many hon. members and to millions of Canadians. While we know that federal officials are competent people we do not accept, as legislators responsible for the political, constitutional and legislative policies of this country, that a committee composed of civil servants, whose names we do not know, be appointed to study constitutional matters.
Many members of this house feel that this responsibility is incumbent on the legislator and that in delaying the setting up of such a committee, the government is fostering the present confusion and conflicts, which is not in the best interests of Canada and does not help to promote understanding between central and provincial governments.
For my part, I am anxious to hear the minister make his statement at the end of this debate and give us some details concerning the correspondence exchanged and the discussions held with representatives of the different provinces. But I see, from the underlying principle of this bill, that the federal government continues to intervene, directly or indirectly, in matters concerning education, since this legislation itself deals with the occupational training of adults.
I understand that the minister has already stated, in speeches and conferences, that it was up to the federal government to provide customers for the provincial authorities and for industry, by taking over all the financial responsibility for the occupational training of adults. The minister will probably tell us that the central government has no intention, through its officials and its agencies, to give 23033-9691
Occupational Training
training and education courses to adults, that this is left to provinces. But this act departs from the spirit and the letter of the Canadian constitution.
Our constitution must be amended, at least reformed and modernized, to keep pace with the progress of science and modern industrial techniques. That is why the government must create this official framework for constitutional reforms.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
That is why it is urgent for the government to set up that official framework for constitutional reform. But no, it is delaying the establishment of that framework and the official reform of the constitution, in agreement with provincial legislators and other Canadians, to continue to invade either directly or indirectly a field which, according to the spirit and the letter of the Canadian constitution, comes under provincial jurisdiction.
Of course, according to section 93 of our constitution, education comes under the exclusive authority of the provinces. It is clearly indicated in section 93 that education comes entirely and exclusively under the provinces.
Courts have been asked to give an interpretation of the word education. I think it was Justice Duff who, in his comments on the word education, wrote that it was used in a wide sense and included all fields of training.
It is also worth remembering that the 72 Quebec resolutions of 1864, which served as the basis for the drafting of the 147 sections of our 1867 constitution, in no way dissociated culture from education, or education from primary, secondary or university education, nor separated academic training from postacademic training; on the contrary, the wording of section 93 of our Canadian constitution gives full authority to the provincial governments.
I know that the minister or other hon. members will say that the central government will not, under this bill, give the courses itself, that it will merely pay the costs and allowances, but the fact is that in judgments rendered by the Privy Councill of London, which was our last court of appeal until 1949, many decisions were favourable to the spirit of a true federalism and recognized the sovereignty and autonomy of the federal government in matters coming under its jurisdiction by virtue of the constitution, but also the sovereignty and autonomy of the provinces in those fields set out in the confederation pact.

Mr. Speaker, I know that the house likes nothing more at this hour of the evening than a legalistic or constitutional homily. Because the house likes such dissertations I am ready to oblige. 1 assure hon. members that my remarks will be brief, but the point is one that should be made, and I welcome the attention the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) is paying to me.
This bill, if and when passed, will confer upon the governor in council power to make certain regulations. That power is specified in various clauses of the bill, with a particular list of such regulations being set out in clause 12. It is standard practice with respect to legislation passed in parliament for us to give the governor in council power, by regulation, to enact certain provisions which have the force of law.
However, one of the cardinal principles of our form of government is that the executive-the cabinet, or the governor in council-does not have authority to legislate except in so far as that authority is given to it by parliament. This is a principle to which lip service and obeisance are often paid; but there have been times in the history of our parliament when that principle has been violated. It is my contention that it has been violated recently by the present government.
I hold in my hand a copy of the adult occupational training regulations which were
April 25. 1967

passed by order in council and which are now in effect. The parliamentary secretary referred to them several times in his speech last night, and they have been referred to a number of times during the debate today.
When one looks at these regulations he realizes that they are the regulations which were intended to be passed under the provisions of Bill C-278 after that bill had been passed. As one looks closely at the regulations he realizes that more is included in them than would have been necessary to include in them, had the passing of the regulations awaited the passage of the bill. As a matter of fact in the regulations one finds, word for word, a repetition of a number of the bill's clauses. In fact the important clauses of the bill are set out verbatim in the regulations.
It is my contention that the government had no legislative authority to enact these regulations. If I may refer back to what I said a few moments ago, I mean that parliament has not by any statute given the government power to enact these regulations.
Last evening when I raised this point by asking a question at the end of the parliamentary secretary's speech, he replied in this fashion, as reported on page 15263 of Hansard for April 24:

Read these regulations again and read the bill which is before us. The government has admitted that because it did not get this bill through it achieved the same end by passing these regulations. I like to see good programs get under way. I agree with those who have said this is an exceedingly important measure. In fact I agree with the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald) who suggested that this was probably the most important bill we have discussed so far this session. But for heaven's sake let us not forget the basic principles upon which government in this country is founded. One of those principles is that the executive does not have the right to legislate except when authority to do so has been specifically given to it by statutes of parliament. My contention is that the government has not got the authority for these regulations, and should not have acted in this way.
What governments do when they get into a position of this kind is to say: Who can stop us? They may not use that language always, though one hon. gentleman did; but in effect that is what they say. They do so because our system also works on the principle that if the government does something wrong all we can

April 25, 1967

do is throw the government out by defeating it on the floor of parliament, or by defeating it at the next election.
Far too often governments are tempted to act in an arbitrary way when they feel something needs to be done as a matter of urgency.
