Mr. Speaker, after listening to five or six hours of debate, I begin to wonder what is probably related to good political tactics, what is perhaps related to the conclusion and what is related to the actual weaknesses of the bill now before the house.
Perhaps, like my good friend for Prince (Mr. MacDonald), when we have gained a little more experience, we can untangle all the aspects of the problems debated in this house.
What struck me, Mr. Speaker, in the comments made, is not so much the criticisms that were made and that were, in most cases, objective and related to real doubts in the minds of hon. members, as the fact that virtually no attention was given to one of the most basic and most revolutionary aspects of the bill under consideration.
In my opinion, and I say this without any partisanship whatsoever, I would be glad to have the House of Commons of Canada accept a principle of this kind, and I think it would justify my presence in Ottawa for the last year and a half, and perhaps for the rest of my life, if I put through, for the first time in Canada, legislation recognizing-and rightly so-that the worker having to retrain due to
Occupational Training
technological changes in industry is entitled to the maintenance of his income and that he has a right to something more than the small allowance to keep him from starving to death. It goes without saying that he is not guaranteed any income enabling him to spend his winters in Florida, but such income will nevertheless be sufficient for him to provide a living for his family, while recognizing that his activity in retraining is normal. That, in my opinion, is basic and I suggest it meets an urgent need of our modern industrial society.
If we had been blamed for not introducing a more perfect bill than the one under consideration, I would have understood, but let us say that the basic principle was a little neglected even by those are said to be in the vanguard. That might be good political tactics; that might be normal; but to me it is so important that I will at least point it out to the house, because it is a precedent that will undoubtedly be used as a basis for a truly human retaining system that will meet today's needs.
I was surprised also at the confusion that seemed to prevail in some minds. I had the impression sometimes that the bill had not been read and that some main points had escaped some hon. members.
Mr. Speaker, it is certain that this bill does not aim at settling once and for all the whole problem of education in Canada, whether it is basic academic training or technical training. Its objective is quite different. That bill does not replace the provincial institutions and does not take any responsibility away from the provinces; it is only determining what will happen on the labour market when the workers need to be retrained.
Obviously, the scope of the bill is much larger than before. Its value was cut down and it was suggested that it was very restrictive whereas in fact, it is quite general in scope.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to refer to some of the objections raised in the house but before I do, I should like to detail the basis or the motivation of the overall policy.
Mr. Speaker, until recently, we had agreements with the provinces through our jurisdiction over occupational training, enabling us to offer training or retraining courses to certain categories of workers. We also had agreements on capital expenditures for the establishment or construction of technical or occupational training schools.
There used to be a sort of dual jurisdiction in the field of occupational instruction. I have

April 25, 1867
Occupational Training
no desire to criticize what has been done at the time and I believe that this legislation has been most useful to Canada. In fact, it was a starting point which enabled us to catch up in building schools and occupational institutions. Even though that act is out of date today, it has nevertheless proved quite useful to the whole country.
We wanted, first of all, to clarify the question of jurisdiction. In this connection, members of the political parties represented in this house will have to take their stand, because it must be determined whether or not the federal government has jurisdiction in the field of occupational training. It seems that our stand must be defined and that the federal government as such has no jurisdiction over educational institutions, over cur-riculums, even in the field of occupational training.
Under the previous scheme, the federal government could negotiate with the provinces, not only with regard to courses but also to the building standards of institutions. We put an end to that, and if the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) can read, he may be able to read it, because he took pleasure in mixing up everything, probably for a forthcoming television program. So, if he can read, he will find that we have withdrawn from that field. As for his reference to two architects arguing about the building of a school, that may have been possible in the past, but not any longer, because the province is now responsible for its own institutions. As a matter of fact, it is the province which will draw up the curriculums, hire the teachers, and plan the occupational training. It is quite clear that this comes under provincial jurisdiction.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
Some hon. members suggest that this bill is a further intrusion of the federal government in the field of education, whereas it is clear that we have withdrawn from education proper. As a matter of fact, under this bill, we accept a responsibility with regard to employment and unemployment in Canada, and since we know that part of that unemployment is due to a lack of vocational training, we are providing those who are unemployed because of technological changes or automation, or simply because their skills are outdated, with the means of acquiring the vocational training they need through courses given by provincial institutions administered by the provinces.
[Mr. Marchand.l
Therefore, when the house is told-as if we understood nothing at all-that this is new and that we will be paying twice for the same services, I say that this is not so. It may have been possible in the past, but not now. Instead of two distinct services, there is the province which provides services in the field of education, and the federal government which assumes its responsibility with regard to employment and which sees to it that workers are able to benefit from the institutions and vocational training courses of the provinces.
Therefore, that point is quite clear, at least in my mind. One may disagree, even with the present intentions of the government, but one should at least recognize that, by comparison to the system which expired an April 1 or March 31, the present scheme certainly respects provincial autonomy to a greater degree.
Mr. Speaker, we have been blamed for not having consulted the provinces, for having proceeded autocratically, because the provinces complained. I know why they complained, and we could perhaps talk about that later on, but this matter of occupational training, as it appears in the bill under consideration, was discussed more than a year ago, at the first federal-provincial conference. It was then discussed in detail at the second federal-provincial conference last October, when the premiers as well as the provincial ministers of education and labour were informed of our intentions. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) explained that new philosophy, after which the officials of the federal Department of Manpower and Immigration and those of the provincial departments met to discuss the terms and regulations. There were exchanges of opinions and, in short, it is after all those consultations, all those exchanges, that we came up with the legislation which is now submitted to the house.
Some people contend that we trampled over the provinces and proceeded in an autocratic way. I believe we should distinguish between the dissatisfaction of the provinces in seeing the old system come to an end and the dissatisfaction expressed under the pretence that we have proceeded too hastily and in an authoritative way, which is not true.

Mr. Speaker, many objections have been made to the fact that some young people will lose under the new plan some of the rights they had under the former one. There again, let us not be misled, for the young people of 17 or 18, who have not attended school for a year, although not entitled to the allowances we have set, can still take the courses free of charge. The case was presented in such a way as to give the impression that under the new plan all those young people will quit the occupational training centres because we have decided that they are not entitled to the allowances. occupational training in provincial schools, and we will pay 100 per cent of the cost.
However, we were faced with the problem of deciding whether we could give them, at the same time, the same allowances as to adults who have family responsibilities and who are part of the labour force.
Let us try for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to consider the effect such an action could have on students if, after being out of school for only one year, they were allowed to go back to school and receive a $35 weekly allowance in addition to their tuition fees. Do you not think we would witness a mass exodus from the schools of young people who would see this as a way of obtaining a salary. In my opinion, this would create an intolerable situation in the schools, because you could have two students with exactly the same status in seats next to each other, and one would be getting $35 a week, and the other nothing. This means that those who continue their studies in high school or beyond would not be eligible for the allowance. They would have to leave school for a year in order to get the $35 a week.
That is not the aim of this legislation. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, its aim is to provide financial help for workers who are legitimately a part of the labour force but who are unemployed and whose professional qualifications are outdated and useless, to help them live during their retraining period.
This legislation is not designed to provide free education in all vocational schools in Canada. That might be a good thing, but it will be done through another legislation.
The object of this bill is especially to grapple with this great evil arising from modern industry, which causes workers to lose not only their trade but their skills. We must endeavour to train them not only once but two, three or four times during their lifetime. That is the object of this clause. Provincial governments are dealt with on an equal footing with everyone else.
Everybody gets the same treatment-women, men, young people-provided one has been connected with the labour market for three years.

nursery schools. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that if Canada does not only accept, but also wishes that women work it will be necessary to create normal working conditions for them. [DOT] (10:40 p.m.)

I am sure the hon. member means well. Unfortunately he has swallowed whole the attitude of the conservatives of the educational establishment. Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) asked for the same thing. Right now we are collecting this correspondence, and we will be happy to table it as soon as this is done. Apart from the official correspondence between the federal government and the provinces, there has also been some correspondence between the regional offices and the provincial governments, and we want to collect all of this. I think that the question of the hon. member was not properly founded as far as we are concerned because he mentioned the withdrawal of the federal government from training courses, which is not true. We never withdrew from anything. The agreements expired on March 31, and we never withdrew from that field. We came back with a new proposal which is before the house right now.
To come back to what I was saying-the results are not very constructive. Of course, those officials have preferred thus to make the same sort of arrangement for the future as came to an end on March 31. The essence of the arrangements was that we gave very large subsidies to whatever program the provinces chose to operate.
The officials concerned were able to say to their treasury boards: "Approve this $100 million program and it will only cost you $25 million or $50 million. The federal government will reimburse you for the rest". Of course the officials like that system, and if a member of the federal government wishes to make himself the mouthpiece for that viewpoint, I suppose he has the right to do so. But as far as I am concerned, the issue at stake here is the interest of the people of Canada.
I think I have shown, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North was kind enough to recognize, that I am fully prepared to improve my policies in response to reasonable criticism. I may say that I have the fullest co-operation of my senior officials in that attitude. However, I am not prepared to change good policies because some people with special interests put on a campaign of bad arguments.
The most common argument advanced against this bill is that it makes a distinction between education and occupational training 23033-9705
Occupational Training
for adults. Bluntly speaking, this argument is nonsense. There has always been a distinction. It used to be that while municipalities and provinces provided free education up to a certain age, they made no provision whatever for adult training. Furthermore, we are not even involved in adult training. All we are doing is to give money to those workers who need retraining. We are not involved in adult education. That began to change when hon. gentlemen opposite were in government. At that time the government introduced the technical and vocational training program. It was a good program for its day. The provinces took advantage of it to build a lot of schools. We have undertaken to spend for that purpose in the future almost as much as has been spent in the past six years. But one of the features of the old program was that it most certainly distinguished between education and training. The assistance given for the operating costs of high schools was strictly limited to a total for the country of $3 million a year out of a program costing in total more than $200 million a year. That $3 million is what we are withdrawing; that is all.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)
Under the old program, as under the new, adult training was supported on quite a different formula and a much bigger scale. Nevertheless the provinces were slow to get into adult training on a large scale. That is the fact to which the Economic Council drew such forcible attention and which no one denies. It is the reason why we changed our policy to provide the whole cost of adult training instead of 50 per cent or 75 per cent depending on the people being trained.
It is true, of course, that educational and training programs should very largely be planned together, that to a considerable extent they use the same physical facilities, and so on. That is obvious. That is why we are not proposing to set up training centres or run training programs. We are going on doing what was done before, only we are doing it on a bigger scale. Instead of financing part of the cost of training for various defined categories of adults we are paying the whole cost for all adults who need training.
I want to make this quite clear. There are no exclusions. Anyone who has been out of school for a year and who was previously entitled to training under a federally supported program is now entitled to training with the whole cost paid by the federal government. The difference is in coverage. Before there were all kinds of exclusions, and now

April 25. 1967
Occupational Training
there are not. That is one important difference between the old program and the new one.
The other main difference is a matter, not of training as such, but of manpower planning. Under the old system we identified a man as needing training and the province then accepted him when it could into one or other of the training courses in which they had a vacancy. There was no necessary relationship between the courses provided and the jobs that were going to be available. In taking 100 per cent financial responsibility we are changing that. We are saying that we will pay the whole cost of training in a course that equips the individual for a job he is likely to be able to get and do.
In the past the attitude tended to be to fill up the courses that were available. Now there will be a much more direct pressure to pattern the courses to meet the employment needs of the individual. That is the change that is disturbing some officials. But I do not think anyone would seriously advance it as an argument against our policy. That is the one difference we are making that affects the relationship between education and training and the structure of training courses.
Financially, from the point of view of the public, which is what matters, we are not creating a distinction between education and training. We are making them more alike. We are accepting the financial responsibility for seeing that free training is available to all adults when they need it, in the same way that free education is available to all children. Finally on this point of the alleged distinction between education and manpower training, let me repeat what I said in October to the federal-provincial conference:
The distinction we do make is quite different. It is not between kinds of education. It is a distinction between the needs of people-between, on the one hand, students in the ordinary sense and, on the other hand, men and women who are or have been earning their livings but who need further training or retraining for productive employment.
That means, of course, that there is one financial distinction. In order to take training most adults need a replacement income. But no province, as far as I know, has proposed to pay an income to the children in its schools. Therefore there is a line to be drawn as to when people should get training allowances. Obviously, if we pay allowances to young people of 17 or so, we create an incentive for them to drop out of school early and take training later.

There was a reference in the debate to whether we had conducted research on this program. For example, we commissioned an independent research firm to investigate student attitudes toward staying in school for the next two years or dropping out to work for a year and then receiving an allowance to take training. The finding was that if the allowances were available after only one year, the drop-out rate in grades 9 and 10 might rise by 40 to 50 per cent. That is the reason for the three-year rule for young people without dependants. It is not because we want to deprive them of their right to be trained. We want them to be trained and we are ready even to pay for their courses, but we are not ready to create an incentive that will probably destroy many school systems in many provinces.
Of course, like most things, it is the lesser of two evils. We would be severely and rightly attacked if we paid allowances to a lot of young people who were thereby encouraged to drop out of school early. On the other hand, of course, there are certainly some young people who had no choice but to leave school and who will be compelled to work, not trained, during the first three years afterwards. But the number of those cases is certainly not the 7,000 that some official has given to the press in Ontario. That is a wild exaggeration. A realistic estimate of the potential trainees who will not be entitled to allowance would be 2,000 to 3,000, and of course by no means all of them will necessarily have to forgo training.
There have been other allegations of discrimination. One hon. member charged discrimination against women. I urge him to read the bill. He will find that a woman just as much as a man will be eligible for our training courses regardless of whether she is married or single or is 30 or 45 years of age or even 20. All that is required is that she be one year out of school, just like men, and for the same reason. She will receive a training allowance if she has dependants or has been working in just the same way as a man.
The same hon. member attempted yesterday to criticize my able parliamentary secretary by claiming yet another type of discrimination, against immigrants. This charge is equally invalid. The bill treats immigrants in the same way as Canadians. An immigrant will be eligible for our training courses if he has been out of school for one year. Indeed, an immigrant youngster of 16 or 17 years of age can be enrolled in our program the day
April 25, 19G7



after he has landed in this country. He or she will receive a training allowance if he or she has been working for at least three years, and we do not make any distinction between working in Canada and working abroad. I am sure that no hon. member would suggest an improvement in these conditions; to do so would be to discriminate against Canadian workers. This applies equally to other special categories of people. We are treating them all exactly alike, on exactly the same principles.
I will turn now to a different issue. It has been alleged that we failed to consult adequately with the provinces. Allow me to state the facts. This is what I said in French: In October last, that is six months ago, this program was a main topic of the federal-provincial conference in Ottawa attended by provincial premiers and provincial ministers of education. This conference was followed a month later by another meeting in Ottawa with the provincial deputy ministers of education and labour at which the new provisions for training adults were discussed in detail. In January and February officials from departmental headquarters travelled to provincial capitals to join our regional officers in discussing the new program with provincial officials. Then and since our regional directors have been in continuing contact with their provincial colleagues.
[DOT] (11:00 p.m.)
The hon. member for Winnipeg North charged my department with rigidity. He claimed that we had not listened to the suggestions from the provinces, and that not one of the principles of the program enunciated earlier had been changed. May I say that by listening to provincial urging the federal treasury became lighter by some $300 million.
At the October conference, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) accepted provincial representations which changed the phasing out formula for capital grants, giving the provinces an additional quarter of a billion dollars. At the subsequent November meeting, the federal government announced a change in the original proposal for the occupational training program for adults so that younger persons with less than three years experience would be included in the training. Under our first proposal they were not even entitled to their tuition fees, and we were not paying anything. We modified that provision, too. As the house will hear at a later stage, we are ready in committee to propose certain amendments to the bill as it stands now, to meet
Occupational Training
some small technical points on which the provinces have advanced good arguments.
It is true that despite this consultation, a great deal of misinformation about the program has appeared in the press, apparently on the authority of one or two provincial officers. I can only say that there are none so deaf as those who do not want to listen. It is quite true that under the new program we will not subsidize some things the provincial departments would like subsidized. We never can satisfy them. When we have refused, we have refused because, in our judgment, there are more important and more appropriate uses for the public funds for which we are responsible. This is a highly expansionist program which opens up the way for a vast improvement in the training available to Canadian workers. I hope it can be discussed and passed in that spirit.

I shall now conclude, Mr. Speaker. There are probably objections to which I have not replied, but I shall have an opportunity to do so when we debate the bill section by section. However, I recall the objection that training allowances could vary from one area to another. That was done precisely at the request of the provinces because, in view of the relatively high level of the allowances, it could happen that, in some areas, allowances are higher than the real wages, and it seemed reasonable, after discussion with the provinces, that we allow some flexibility in that respect.
Therefore, I would prefer, as many people do, that salaries be equal in Canada, from one area to another-I am sure it would be better that way. We have not worked such a miracle yet. Trade unions have not accomplished it and employers obviously do not wish it either. But, in any event, we are taking into account the situation as it is.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the bill before us now-I am not saying it is perfect, nor that we will not have to change it a year from now-is one that is in the forefront of legislation in that field and that the house, instead of delaying it, for the sake of delaying should hasten to put it into force so that the workers may take advantage of it as soon as possible, not only the workers, but the Canadian economy as a whole, even if we have to amend it later, for we will probably realize that there are defects, that from the administrative point of view, there might be difficulties and no doubt also that we will want to extend it.

April 25. 1967

But in regard to the principle ot a bill such as this it would be hard to understand, Mr. Speaker, that the House of Commons would not agree to give it a fair trial.

It is the speech made yesterday by his parliamentary secretary, while the minister was speaking about the horse and the fly in the riding of Lapointe. It would have been better for the minister to be in the house to see what was going on when such an important legislation was introduced. The parliamentary secretary repeated many times the following words: the funds that we will pay to the provinces for the training of adults will enable them to repay interest and principal. That means a new administration set-up. That means the federal controller would do exactly the same thing as did the provincial controller. And it is like that everywhere. Double expenses. And that, Mr. Chairman, to be told what? To be told by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, who advocated not so

long ago, as he was militating in the unions: Freedom of the unions. Such flabbergasting words one must hear from other people. The individuals are not the ones who will decide what course they will be taking, they will be consulted, I admit, but they will not be the ones to decide, the manpower official will do that, not the individual, no. Oh no. He may show natural dispositions or wish to work in such or such a field, or express his wish to the official if he wants to, but it will be up to the official to make the decision.
Mr. Chairman, what kind of freedom is that? Is that the way the minister always fought for the workers in the past? What will the workers say in the province of Quebec, when they will be told this: You want occupational training, very well, you will not decide about it, it will be up to the bureaucrat or to the official to make the decision.

Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment to make to clause 1. I move that:
Clause 1 of Bill S-10, an act respecting Inter-provinclal Pipe Line Company is deleted and the following clause substituted therein:
"1. Notwithstanding anything contained in section 3 of chapter 34 of the statutes of 1949 (1st session), as amended by chapter 66 of the statutes of 1952-53,

The purpose of this amendment is to meet objections previously raised to the capitalization which appears in the first sentence of the explanatory notes of the bill, namely 40 million shares, and reduces that capitalization by half.

I know there has been a great deal of concern on the part of some people with regard to this particular bill. I agree with those who say, why pick on Interprovincial? The sponsor of the bill and the board of directors of the company have been able to remove what had become an unwieldy treasury issue of stock, with stock being issued but there being no intention of putting this stock out to raise money which the company may need for expansion. It seems to me that this has eliminated one of the things to which I took objection. I believe, however, the company would be poorly advised to come back within the next four or five years requesting an additional stock split because I think we might not be as lenient the next time.

So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, this bill is asking this house to grant an open hunting licence, as I would call it and as it has been called by others in the oil industry, since the company has not established any particular plan for any pipe line.
This bill presumably authorizes at some time or other the construction of a pipe line to connect with the provincial pipe line now under construction in the Rainbow Lake area of northwestern Alberta. However, under this proposal the pipe line could be extended into the Northwest Territories and would therefore come under the jurisdiction of this parliament and the National Energy Board.
Because of the complexities and peculiar nature of oil exploration and development in this particular area, there is great fear that once the pipe line was built by this corporation, which is actually owned by a consortium of major oil companies, any independents would be precluded from oil development in the Northwest Territories. This is something to which I do not think we should bar the door.
It is true that this extensive oil development in western Canada has resulted from the operations of the major oil companies. They have done by far the biggest development; but we should not shut out the independents. There is another independent pipe line company which could also reach into this area.
There is no evidence on record, as far as I can ascertain, that gives us sufficient information to consider this bill and accept it; therefore it must go to committee. I have sufficient doubt about this proposal at this time that I am not prepared to let the bill go through on the present basis without a clearer indication from the proposers of what they intend to do. This is almost the granting of a carte blanche to a company owned by major oil concerns under foreign ownership to operate into the Northwest Territories, and perhaps even into the Yukon.
